1	## 2. What the research found
2	
3	Chapter 1 showed a large, treatable population, a system that loses half of it between visits, and a market that stops before the dose. This chapter condenses what the research found, in plain words. It starts with the clinical evidence on what actually improves outcomes, then turns to how others have scaled care without specialists, what the technology can and cannot do, who is already doing this, where the money is and what the rules allow.
4	
5	### 2.1 What actually improves outcomes
6	
7	> **In short.**
8	> - Outcomes improved when a home reading led to a changed treatment, and mostly did not when the reading was only shown or turned into a reminder.
9	> - Who was allowed to change the dose mattered more than the electronics.
10	> - Raising adherence on its own did not move outcomes.
11	> - The same pattern holds in diabetes, heart failure, warfarin and asthma, and the known harms of dose stepping can be met with stop rules.
12	
13	The trials sort into five rules. OUR VIEW: the sorting is ours; the numbers are from the notes.
14	
15	**Rule 1. The reading must change the treatment.** Across 15 pooled trials (7,138 people, 12 months), self-monitoring of blood pressure alone lowered systolic pressure (the upper number, in mmHg, millimetres of mercury) by 1.0 mmHg against usual care: no effect. With intensive support (dose changes by doctors, pharmacists or patients, plus education or counselling), not dose changes alone, it fell 6.1 mmHg [D1-01-F05]. Where the dose itself moved, the falls were larger. In the UK trial TASMIN-SR (552 high-risk patients, randomised, meaning people got each treatment by chance), patients stepping their own dose by an agreed plan had systolic pressure 9.2 mmHg lower than under usual care at 12 months [D1-01-F02]. In the US trial HyperLink (450 patients, 16 clinics randomised as clusters, meaning whole clinics rather than single patients), pharmacists adjusting drugs from home readings got 57.2% controlled against 30.0% with usual care [D1-01-F04]. An independent US review by the Peterson Health Technology Institute (PHTI, October 2024) rated monitoring-only programmes "not clinically meaningful" and programmes where care teams adjust drugs "clinically meaningful and more rapid", against a threshold of a 5 mmHg fall in systolic pressure [D1-01-F39].
16	
17	![Extra fall in systolic pressure against usual care, by what was done with the reading](adaptive-care-pictures/20-what-lowers-pressure.png)
18	
19	*Chart: separate trials with different patients and end points, so compare the groups, not single bars [D1-01-F01, D1-01-F02, D1-01-F03, D1-01-F04, D1-01-F05, D1-01-F06, D1-01-F07].*
20	
21	**Rule 2. Who is allowed to decide matters more than the electronics.** In the UK trial TASMINH4 (1,182 patients, 12 months), the family doctor adjusted doses in every arm, and sending home readings electronically instead of on paper added 1.2 mmHg, not significant (small enough to be chance) [D1-01-F03]. In rural China, the China Rural Hypertension Control Project (CRHCP: 326 villages, 33,995 people aged 40 and over) let village doctors start and step drugs by a standard protocol under physician supervision. At 18 months, 57.0% were under 130/80 against 19.9% with enhanced usual care [D1-01-F09]. After a median of 4 years, cardiovascular events were lower, with a hazard ratio (a risk ratio over time; below 1 means fewer events) of 0.75 at age 60 and over and 0.64 under 60. The programme also gave free or discounted drugs and paid village doctors incentives tied to control rates, so the effect cannot be credited to the protocol alone [D1-01-F38].
22	
23	India has the null result that belongs here. mWellcare (40 community health centres, 3,698 people with hypertension, diabetes or both, 12 months, randomised by centre) gave nurses and doctors an app that prompted treatment steps during visits. Against enhanced usual care the systolic difference was 0.98 mmHg, not significant; both arms fell by about 13 mmHg [D1-01-F46]. OUR VIEW: it shows that a prompt at a visit adds nothing to a well-run protocol programme. It does not show that dose changes between visits fail: the app did not act on home readings or reach patients who never came back, and no Indian randomised trial of home readings driving a dose protocol was found (D1-01, NOT FOUND list).
24	
25	![Share of patients under control with and without a programme that steps the dose](adaptive-care-pictures/21-share-controlled.png)
26	
27	*Chart: three settings where someone other than a specialist was allowed to step the dose. The China programme also gave free or cheaper medicines and paid for results; the India figures are before and after among the 51% who returned, with no comparison group [D1-01-F04, D1-01-F09, D1-03-F10].*
28	
29	**Rule 3. Adherence technology alone does not move outcomes.** Smart pillboxes or medication labels for tuberculosis (ASCENT, 23,483 patients, four countries) did not reduce poor outcomes against standard care [D1-02-F59]. Inhaler reminders for 220 New Zealand children raised adherence to 84% against 30% over 6 months, with no difference in school absence [D1-02-F01]. A blood-pressure reminder app (MedISAFE-BP, 411 US adults, 12 weeks) moved systolic pressure by 0.5 mmHg, not significant [D1-01-F06]. OUR VIEW: raising a dose that is not being taken is unsafe, so adherence is an input to the dose decision, not a product.
30	
31	**Rule 4. Someone must pay for the outcome.** Chapter 1.5 told this side: apps and sensors sold on their own failed, while the firms that lasted are paid by employers and insurers, or sell a device that delivers the therapy.
32	
33	**Rule 5. People stay when their own clinician is in it.** In eight remote US studies (over 1,00,000 participants), median retention was 5.5 days; referral by a clinician added 40 days, and payment 22 days (one study) [D1-02-F27]. OUR VIEW: a consumer app is the wrong shape.
34	
35	#### What the loop changes, by kind
36	
37	| What the loop changes | Home signal | Proof | Who decides |
38	|---|---|---|---|
39	| 1. Drug dose or protocol step | Cuff, fasting sugar, INR (a blood test of clotting time), weight | Strong | Patient on an agreed plan, pharmacist, nurse or health worker |
40	| 2. Food and behaviour | Glucose sensor, step count | Mixed | App, coach |
41	| 3. Exercise as the dose | Camera, pulse, effort rating | Matches in-person care | Therapist or app |
42	| 4. Therapy delivered by the device (closed-loop insulin pump) | Glucose sensor | Strong | Algorithm, within limits a clinician sets [D1-05-F41] |
43	| 5. Biofeedback (a body signal shown back to the patient) | Breathing or pulse sensor | Weak | Patient |
44	
45	OUR VIEW: proof is strongest in kinds 1 and 4, where a drug dose with a known effect is changed and the signal is cheap, valid and fast. Kind 4 needs expensive hardware; kind 1 needs almost none.
46	
47	#### The evidence by condition
48	
49	| Condition | What works (headline) | Main caution |
50	|---|---|---|
51	| Blood pressure | Dose stepping from home readings by the patient, a pharmacist or a village doctor (rules 1 and 2); strongest proof, up to hard outcomes at 4 years | Leg swelling 32% against 22% with self-titration in TASMINH2 [D1-01-F01]; the China gain came with free drugs and incentives |
52	| Type 2 diabetes | A device computing the next insulin dose (d-Nav, 181 US adults, 6 months, against clinician support alone): HbA1c down 1.0 point against 0.3, with equal low-sugar events; several authors were maker-linked [D1-01-F13] | Low blood sugar. PHTI (March 2024) found US type 2 tools without a continuous glucose monitor "do not deliver clinically meaningful benefits" [D1-01-F40] |
53	| Heart failure | Fast dose stepping after discharge (STRONG-HF, 1,078 patients, 14 countries, against usual care): readmission or death at 180 days an adjusted 15.2% against 23.3% [D1-01-F27] | More side effects (41% against 29%), four visits in two months, lab tests. Telemonitoring without a mandated dose protocol was null in two US trials (1,653 and 1,437 patients) [D1-01-F32, D1-01-F33] |
54	| Warfarin (a blood thinner) | Testing INR at home and setting one's own dose: clots risk ratio (risk with treatment divided by risk without) 0.47 and deaths 0.55 against usual care; leaving the dose to the clinic gave no fewer deaths (0.94) [D1-02-F05] | The two approaches were not compared head to head |
55	| Asthma | Each reliever puff also raises the steroid dose (SMART): flare-ups risk ratio 0.68 (16 trials, 22,748 people), with no sensor [D1-02-F37] | A sensor inhaler system's benefit interval crossed 1 [D1-02-F02] |
56	
57	Other areas repeat the pattern. Nurses stepping gout drugs to a target worked with no software at all [D1-02-F06]; tele-rehabilitation matches in-person care but does not beat usual care [D1-02-F03, D1-02-F07]; and guided breathing for blood pressure showed no effect once maker-linked trials were removed [D1-02-F11].
58	
59	**Prescription apps and safety.** Software sold as a prescribed treatment has passed trials, yet most of the companies behind it failed (chapter 1.5), and none of the prescription apps in the research note changes a drug dose. The closest, Japan's CureApp HT, coaches lifestyle: in 390 untreated adults over 12 weeks it lowered 24-hour systolic pressure 2.4 mmHg more than lifestyle advice alone [D1-01-F07]. OUR VIEW: dose stepping by protocol has a good safety record when the protocol has stop rules. At 4 years in rural China, injurious falls, symptomatic low blood pressure, fainting and kidney outcomes did not differ between groups [D1-01-F38], and insulin-dose proposals in TeleDiab-2 (191 adults, 4 months) caused no severe low blood sugar [D1-01-F14]. The known costs, more minor side effects, leg swelling and low blood sugar, each need their own safety branch.
60	
61	### 2.2 How care has been scaled without specialists
62	
63	> **In short.**
64	> - India's programme already has a protocol, free drugs, a record and an overdue list; the dose step still waits for a doctor's visit.
65	> - Patients who keep attending do well on the protocol; the loss is among those who stop coming.
66	> - Abroad, the largest gains came where a non-doctor could step the dose, with free drugs or one pill.
67	> - Software was part of every working programme and the whole of none.
68	
69	Chapter 2.1 showed that changing the dose works. This section asks how it has been delivered at scale without specialists.
70	
71	#### India's hypertension programme in practice
72	
73	IHCI runs a state protocol of 3 to 4 steps, amlodipine first (chapter 4.1 gives one state's steps); Punjab and Maharashtra order the steps differently at the second step [D3-05-F01, D1-06-F01, D1-06-F02]. Drugs are free, as 30-day refills at every facility level from health and wellness centres to district hospitals [D3-05-F02]. The open-source Simple app takes about 80 seconds to register a patient and 15 seconds for a follow-up, lists overdue patients with high-risk ones first, and offers one-click nurse calls and automated reminders [D3-05-F03]. Medical officers start amlodipine and review at 30 days; nurses register patients and record follow-up [D3-05-F06].
74	
75	For patients who keep coming, the protocol works: in Punjab and Maharashtra, 70% and 76% of patients seen again were controlled on amlodipine 5 mg alone, and 75% and 81% after step 2 [D3-05-F04]. Across 159,292 patients who returned and stayed on protocol, control on clinic readings plateaued at 77% and 82%; about 43% of starters are missing from that count [D1-06-F04]. The drugs are cheap: amlodipine for the first two steps cut drug cost about 20%, from US$2.50 to US$2.05 per patient per year, not counting staff [D3-05-F05].
76	
77	OUR VIEW: IHCI already has the protocol, free drugs, a record and an overdue list. It lacks a dose decision for the uncontrolled patient who does not go back to the doctor (chapter 1.3).
78	
79	**Who changes the dose in practice.** Besides the refill rule in chapter 1.3, search summaries (only) say that state protocol text has the medical officer start and raise the dose, while the ANM (auxiliary nurse midwife) gives a month's medicines once pressure is controlled [D3-05-F31], and that a CHO (community health officer) screens, refers and follows up [D3-05-F30, D3-05-F13]. Whether a nurse or health officer may change a dose in law is open (chapter 2.6). OUR VIEW: design for a doctor approving every dose change.
80	
81	**Tamil Nadu's doorstep scheme.** Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam, launched in August 2021, reported 1,86,13,872 beneficiaries by August 2024, with 92,59,821 people with hypertension given medicines (government figures, not audited; THEIR CLAIM) [D3-05-F14]. It refills; it does not step: no source says the dose is changed at the door [D3-05-F15]. OUR VIEW: high treatment with low control (chapter 1.2) is the gap a dose step addresses.
82	
83	#### Programmes outside India
84	
85	| Programme, size | Who steps the dose | Also in the package | Result |
86	|---|---|---|---|
87	| China rural project (CRHCP) | Village doctors by protocol, physician-supervised | Free or discounted drugs; pay on control rate; audit; free home cuffs (search summary only) [D3-05-F21] | Chapter 2.1 |
88	| Lesotho; 103 villages, 547 people | Lay village health workers, by app | One fixed-dose pill | Under 140/90 at 12 months 58% against 48% (cluster trial against facility referral) [D3-05-F24] |
89	| IMPACT-BP, South Africa; 774 people | Nurses, remotely by app (not stated explicitly) | Health worker collects readings at home and delivers medicine | Systolic 7.9-9.1 mmHg lower at 6 months against standard care [D3-05-F27] |
90	| Nigeria; 60 centres, 21,922 people | Health workers under standing orders (search summary only) | Free drugs, then a US$1.60 co-pay a month; single pills; steady stock | Control 21.7% to 55.9% (2020-2023), no comparison group [D3-05-F22, D3-05-F23] |
91	| COBRA-BPS, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Sri Lanka; 2,645 people | Trained physicians; health workers monitored and referred | Home visits, counselling | Systolic 5.2 mmHg lower at 24 months (cluster trial) [D1-01-F37] |
92	| CARRS, India and Pakistan; 1,146 people with diabetes | Physicians, with software prompts | Care coordinators calling monthly | Combined target 18.2% against 8.7% at 28 months [D3-05-F18] (another note gives 8.1% for the comparison arm [D2-03-F14]); the chance of improving HbA1c, blood pressure and LDL cholesterol together doubled, risk ratio 2.1 at 12 months [D1-01-F23] |
93	
94	OUR VIEW: the largest gains in control came where a non-doctor could step the dose, with free drugs or one pill; monitoring, counselling or prompts gained less or nothing. What these programmes changed, and software alone could not, was drug stock, authority for a non-doctor to change drugs (the PAHO HEARTS roadmap across 33 countries names nurse dose adjustment [D3-05-F28]), a person carrying medicine home, pay linked to control, and a person who phones and books visits. Software was part of every working programme and the whole of none.
95	
96	### 2.3 What the technology can and cannot do
97	
98	> **In short.**
99	> - A home reading can be several mmHg wrong for reasons unrelated to the cuff, such as posture; trusting it is the hard engineering.
100	> - Every working dose algorithm caps its actions and falls back to a standing plan when data is missing.
101	> - Language models make dose errors even when told to follow a protocol; they can read and speak, but should not decide.
102	> - Learning each patient's response is later work: no open data or simulator exists for blood-pressure drugs.
103	
104	If changing the treatment is what works, the technology questions narrow to two: can a home reading be trusted, and can a decision be kept within safe bounds. OUR VIEW: the hard engineering is in trusting the home reading and in bounding the decision, not in the model that makes it.
105	
106	#### Trusting a home reading
107	
108	The American and European hypertension societies publish rules for home readings: how long to rest, how many readings, over how many days, and a lower threshold at home than in clinic; chapter 4.3 applies them [D2-02-F10, D2-02-F11, D2-01-F1]. Small mistakes move the number:
109	
110	| Mistake | Effect, systolic / diastolic (mmHg) |
111	|---|---|
112	| Arm on the lap instead of on a desk | +3.9 / +4.0 (randomised crossover trial, 133 people, Baltimore) [D2-02-F16] |
113	| Arm hanging at the side | +6.5 / +4.4 (same trial) |
114	| Back not supported; legs crossed | +5 to +15 / +6; +5 to +8 / +3 to +5 (American Heart Association) [D2-02-F18] |
115	| Regular cuff on an arm that needs a large or an extra-large one | +4.8 or +19.5 systolic (randomised crossover trial, 195 people) [D2-02-F19] |
116	
117	Noise has already hurt an Indian trial. SMARThealth India (a stepped-wedge cluster trial, in which groups of patients start the programme one after another; 18 clusters, rural Andhra Pradesh) found no blood-pressure effect, partly because "fluctuating BP values" made risk scores disagree, so only 37.2% of the cohort was exposed [D2-03-F17].
118	
119	Getting the number in is also hard. No cuff sold in India was confirmed to use the standard Bluetooth blood-pressure service [D2-02-F3]. A purpose-trained reader of cuff-screen photos reached mean errors of 1.2/0.8 mmHg on 776 US images, but 82% of 7,205 images in a Guatemalan set were poor quality, and only Omron screens were tested [D2-02-F4]. No published test of a general vision-language model on these screens was found [D2-02-F8]. A Bluetooth home cuff, the Omron HEM-7156T, costs about ₹2,600 (2026 listings ₹2,593-3,500; search summary only) [D1-06-F31]. Cuffless blood pressure is not ready: the FDA cleared one cuffless monitor in July 2025 [D2-02-F23], but the European Society of Hypertension says there are "no generally accepted protocols" for validating such devices [D2-02-F25].
120	
121	OUR VIEW: blood pressure is the one signal a household can measure with a validated, cheap device. Cuffless error is about the size of a dose step, so dose decisions stay on cuff readings, and every photo read must be shown back to the patient to confirm.
122	
123	#### Algorithms that set a dose
124	
125	Every dose algorithm in use is bounded. The do-it-yourself insulin system OpenAPS writes its safety rules down: it acts only through temporary basal rates, so if it stops, the pump returns to the normal plan; the rate is capped by the lowest of several limits, including "4x the current scheduled basal rate"; and missing or conflicting data sends it back to the pre-set plan [D2-03-F46]. The American Diabetes Association's 2025 insulin rule steps the dose every 3 days towards a fasting target and lowers it 10-20% after an unexplained low [D1-06-F16]; India's ICMR workflow gives targets but no titration schedule [D1-06-F17]. Blood-pressure ladders use fixed steps with a 30-day review, lab and pregnancy guards and referral at the end (chapter 4.1) [D1-06-F14].
126	
127	People do differ. PHYSIC (randomised, double-blind, repeated crossover, 280 people, Sweden) found real between-person differences in drug response, worth about 4.4 mmHg if the drug were chosen per person [D2-03-F12], while a one-time "responder" label did not predict 12-month response in 608 Chinese patients [D2-03-F13]. OUR VIEW: every working dose algorithm caps its actions and falls back to a standing plan when data is missing; a ladder is the simplest case, and PHYSIC is the honest reason a later learning layer could add value.
128	
129	#### A protocol as data, and decision support in India
130	
131	A protocol written as data, not code, can be read by a clinician, tested branch by branch and swapped without changing the engine. No ready standard fits: WHO SMART Guidelines have no general hypertension kit [D2-03-F50]. Testing is the hard part: when the US VA re-encoded its hypertension decision support (ATHENA-HTN), 26 decision points gave 3,120 possible outputs, and 100 test cases covered "only 1% of the possible output combinations" [D2-03-F55].
132	
133	Indian trials of decision support for clinicians are mixed. CARRS (chapter 2.2) was positive with care coordinators; mWellcare (chapter 2.1) [D2-03-F15] and SMARThealth (above) were null. IMPACT Diabetes (cluster randomised, 418 people, 9 months) gave ASHAs (village health workers) a tablet tool under physician supervision: HbA1c fell by 0.5 or more in 21.8% against 10.3% with usual care [D2-03-F18, D3-04-F17]. OUR VIEW: decision support alone did not beat a well-run programme in two Indian trials, so an engine must act between visits, not prompt during them, and ATHENA's 1% says to test on generated cases and replayed data, not only hand-written ones.
134	
135	#### What language models may and may not do with doses
136	
137	GPT-4, prompted with a hospital tacrolimus protocol on 300 simulated cases, made 13.9% "sentinel errors" in its first version; with stronger constraints and output checks the rate fell to 1.0%, and 13.3% of runs were not reproducible (OUR ARITHMETIC: 100 - 86.7) [D2-03-F38]. No completed randomised trial of a language-model coach with a blood-pressure or HbA1c outcome was found; two are registered [D2-03-F44]. Of the health models the large labs have built, only MedGemma, PaPaGei and HealthBench can be downloaded, and none sets doses [D2-03-F32, D2-03-F28, D2-03-F33].
138	
139	OUR VIEW, following [D2-03-F38, D2-03-F40, D2-03-F46]: the model handles language only (reading the cuff photo, translation, speech); a fixed, tested engine makes every decision from the protocol file; code checks every output against the protocol; and a clinician approves every change.
140	
141	#### Later work
142	
143	Adaptive nudging, which learns when and what to send each person, has one head-to-head win, on steps, not on a clinical measure (DIAMANTE, 168 people, US) [D2-03-F10]. A "digital twin" (a model of one person that predicts their response) is further off for blood-pressure drugs. No open model of that response, no titration simulator, no open type 2 diabetes simulator and no large open dataset of home readings with medicine changes was found [D1-06-F42, D1-06-F43, D1-06-F30]. What can be tested on now is the programme's control-by-step figures [D1-06-F04] and open home blood-pressure series (the R `bp` package, GPL-3) [D2-03-F61]. OUR VIEW: each approved step in a loop gives one labelled example, readings before and 30 days after, which is the dataset a response model would need.
144	
145	### 2.4 Who is already doing this
146	
147	> **In short.**
148	> - In India, many programmes coach around a sensor; the one product found that changes a dose is a drug maker's insulin app of unknown status.
149	> - Abroad, lasting businesses are paid by employers, insurers or health systems, or sell a device that delivers the dose.
150	> - The nearest relatives of a home dose loop are a US company whose software is in a regulator's pilot, a UK company now wound up, and a Japanese cuff maker's UK tool.
151	> - Most money abroad goes to products that show data or coach; no funded home blood-pressure dose-step service was found.
152	
153	Chapter 1.5 told why the market has not fixed the gap. This section maps who is in it, by adaptive depth.
154	
155	#### India
156	
157	Deepest first, as found on 13 Nov 2026. Traction figures are THEIR CLAIM.
158	
159	| Player | Depth | What it changes | Status |
160	|---|---|---|---|
161	| Sanofi My Dose Coach | 4 | Basal insulin dose from a clinician-set plan; given free | India status unknown in 2026 [D1-04-F09] |
162	| Tracky | 3 (claims to support titration; no algorithm shown) | Supports clinician titration of GLP-1 medicines (weight-loss injections) | Launched 23 Mar 2026 [D1-04-F27] |
163	| Twin Health, Sugar.fit, BeatO, Fitterfly, HealthifyRx | 3 | Food and activity plans; HealthifyRx a doctor-set tirzepatide dose; BeatO doctor-led diabetes and GLP-1 programmes | Alive; BeatO claims "2 million+ patients" [D1-04-F01, D1-04-F04, D1-04-F05, D1-04-F06, D1-04-F07, D1-04-F26] |
164	| Lupin Lyfe | 3 | Home cardiac rehabilitation; remote drug change not stated | Says it holds a CDSCO Class C licence, Apr 2024 (THEIR CLAIM) [D1-04-F15, D1-04-F16] |
165	| IHCI with the Simple app; Lupin Adhero, Cipla Spirofy, Dr Reddy's Nerivio | 2 | Fixed protocol and reminders; inhaler and migraine reminders and alerts, no dose change | Alive [D1-04-F19, D1-04-F25, D1-04-F12, D1-04-F18] |
166	| Libre, Ultrahuman, Dozee, Swaasa, Neodocs, Agatsa, Sunfox | 1 | Reading or screening only | Alive [D1-04-F33, D1-04-F20, D1-04-F29, D1-04-F31] |
167	
168	Shut or sold, besides PhableCare (chapter 1.5): Wellthy Therapeutics (coaching, depth 3), whose "additional financing" in June 2023 was led by Beyond Next Ventures [D3-06-F01], was bought by TruDoc on 13 Feb 2024, price undisclosed [D1-04-F21, D2-05-F14]. Fitterfly was bought by PB Health, an insurance-linked firm, in Nov 2025, price undisclosed [D2-05-F35].
169	
170	Searches for remote blood-pressure titration found only Phable (shut) and two trial records [D1-04-F23]; searches for licensed digital therapeutics found only Lyfe and Huma, with the CDSCO register itself not searched [D1-04-F30]. Searches for insulin titration found only My Dose Coach, and searches for inhaler plans, home heart-failure and kidney care, WhatsApp dose changes and GLP-1 dose companions found none that changes the dose. This was one agent's limited search, not proof of absence.
171	
172	#### Abroad
173	
174	Scaled companies abroad are paid by employers, insurers or health systems, or sell a device that delivers the therapy (chapter 1.5 gave Hinge Health and Insulet). Omada (US), paid by employers, plans and health systems, had revenue of $91.3M from 1,134,000 members in the quarter to 30 Sep 2026 and is listed and profitable [D1-05-F12, D1-05-F13]. Virta (US), where clinicians cut medicines, says its revenue is above $160M a year (THEIR CLAIM, Sep 2025) [D1-05-F18].
175	
176	#### The nearest relatives
177	
178	No funded startup of 2025 or 2026 was found whose funding page describes home blood-pressure dose steps by protocol. The nearest are these.
179	
180	- **Cadence (US).** Remote vital signs for older adults; supervised AI agents support medicine changes under the partner medical group's protocols, and health systems pay; how far the AI decides alone is not stated. It raised a $100M Series C in June 2026 [D2-06-F1] and reports 100,000+ active patients and blood-pressure control up 70% relative (THEIR CLAIM) [D2-06-F2]. On 13 Aug 2026 it said its HypertensionOS, protocol-bound titration software for blood-pressure medicines, was selected for the FDA's TEMPO pilot, which "does not constitute FDA approval or clearance" (THEIR CLAIM) [D3-06-F31]. PHTI had named Cadence among the programmes where a team adjusts medicine [D1-05-F1].
181	- **Closed Loop Medicine (UK).** Its one blood-pressure trial (published 2024, company and university authors) adjusted amlodipine through an app in 205 adults over 14 weeks, with no comparison group; systolic fell 11 mmHg [D3-06-F09]. It also launched GLP-1 dose options for clinicians in the US (WeDosify, 18 Sep 2025) [D2-06-F24]. The company has been in members' voluntary liquidation (a solvent winding-up by shareholders) since 28 Apr 2026 [D3-06-F07].
182	- **Omron (Japan), in the UK.** The cuff maker's Hypertension Plus collates home readings and drafts a medication plan that the clinician accepts or modifies (search summary only; THEIR CLAIM) [D3-06-F35].
183	
184	#### Prescribed apps and funded companies abroad
185	
186	Germany is the one country with years of numbers on apps that doctors prescribe and public insurers pay for (called DiGA): about 1.9 million prescriptions in 2020-2025 [D1-05-F27], about EUR 400M paid by insurers in five years [D1-05-F28], and an average negotiated price of EUR 227 across 40 apps [D1-05-F29]; 18 of 81 listed apps were removed for lack of proven benefit (Sep 2026) [D1-05-F25]. Japan insures CureApp HT (chapter 2.6), but its prescription counts were NOT FOUND [D1-05-F36]. OUR VIEW: public payers will pay for prescribed apps, but increasingly for results.
187	
188	Among 32 companies funded or launched abroad, the largest rounds went to Function ($298M), Hippocratic AI ($126M), Cadence and Nourish ($100M each), and only Cadence describes medicine changes [D2-06-F42, D2-06-F20, D2-06-F5]. Blood-pressure money buys sensors, not decisions: Biobeat, Aktiia and Vital Signals raised $50M, $42M and $15M+ for products that only show readings [D2-06-F36, D2-06-F37, D2-06-F38]. Only three of the 32 are clearly at depth 4 (Cadence, Twin Health and WeDosify). The frontier AI labs' consumer health features of 2026, such as ChatGPT Health (7 Jan) and Claude's health connectors (11 Jan), read phone health data and change no treatment [D2-06-F15, D2-06-F16]. None of the Y Combinator and a16z lines read mentions dose titration by rule [D2-06-F47, D2-06-F49, D2-06-F50].
189	
190	OUR VIEW, the gap: abroad the pattern exists inside broad virtual clinics paid by US payers and for weight-loss medicines, and the low-income-country programmes found are protocol care, not device-linked dose loops [D1-05-F65]. Nobody funded sells a blood-pressure dose loop for a public programme run by health workers. These are one night's search results: a hospital, drug maker or state may run something unpublished.
191	
192	### 2.5 The money
193	
194	> **In short.**
195	> - Most money in blood-pressure care goes to medicines; a service priced near a pill would double the patient's bill, so usually someone else must pay.
196	> - No Indian payer was found for remote monitoring or digital therapy; our view is that a private clinic or hospital chain is the likeliest first payer.
197	> - On our own arithmetic the reachable Indian market is real but small for a venture fund, and the US$100 million-a-year test fails on India alone.
198	> - Indian chronic-care firms in the notes lose money; the profitable foreign ones are paid by employers and plans.
199	
200	Chapter 1.5 showed who pays today. This section follows the rupee further.
201	
202	#### What is spent today
203	
204	India's retail medicine market was ₹2,45,943 crore in the year to March 2026 [D2-05-F02]. Blood-pressure medicines sold about ₹16,371 crore at retail chemists in the year to December 2025 (not hospital tenders or Jan Aushadhi; the page does not label the period explicitly) [D2-05-F01]. One amlodipine plus telmisartan 5/40 pill a day had a median price of ₹10.7 a tablet for a private brand, ₹1.5 for a Jan Aushadhi generic and ₹0.59 in the public programme (2019-20 prices). The private brand comes to about ₹3,906 a year, about ₹325 a month (OUR ARITHMETIC: ₹10.7 x 365); that is the cost of one brand pill, not a measured patient spend, and the paper's private range is about ₹2,500-5,100 a year [D2-05-F17]. No measured public-private split of treatment was found; a 2021 letter assumed 30% public [D2-05-F30]. OUR VIEW: a service near the price of one combination pill doubles the bill, so usually someone else must pay.
205	
206	#### Who could pay in India
207	
208	| Payer | What the notes have | Would they pay (OUR VIEW) |
209	|---|---|---|
210	| Patients | Chapter 1.5 | Some urban patients will; a monthly fee on top of medicines is hard for most |
211	| Clinics and hospital chains | The private sector gives about 70% of all outpatient care (authors' statement, 2021) [D3-07-F03] | Yes, if the loop keeps patients and refills inside their system |
212	| Medicine makers | Patient-support budgets NOT FOUND [D2-05-F40] | Possible, but a maker that sells the drug being stepped up has a conflict |
213	| Insurers | IRDAI's 2024 master circular says insurers should offer chronic and outpatient cover but does not mandate it [D2-04-F33] | Not yet: almost no outpatient cover |
214	| Employers | Could not be confirmed | Possible, with a slow sales cycle |
215	| States | Chapters 1.3 and 1.5; AB-PMJAY pays for hospital care only (search summary only) [D2-04-F47] | Largest pool, lowest price; only for proven results |
216	
217	OUR VIEW: the first payer is a private clinic or hospital chain. Insurers become a payer only after outcome data exist.
218	
219	#### Market size, counted two ways
220	
221	All figures here are OUR ARITHMETIC from our market model, in rupees a year, at ₹149 a patient a month, ₹1,788 a year (ASSUMPTION, from the build plan). Each level is counted top-down and bottom-up, and the lower figure is used so the case does not rest on the kinder count.
222	
223	![Market size, counted two ways](adaptive-care-pictures/23-market-size.png)
224	
225	*Chart: the levels used after counting each two ways. OUR ARITHMETIC; several inputs are assumptions.*
226	
227	| Level | Top-down | Bottom-up | Used (the lower) |
228	|---|---|---|---|
229	| TAM (total market): Indian adults on blood-pressure medicines | ₹7,494 crore (419.1 lakh private retail patients) | ₹9,969 crore (557.5 lakh treated adults, low case) | **₹7,494 crore** |
230	| SAM (the part we could serve): private patients a doctor could enrol on a household smartphone | ₹1,668 crore (93.3 lakh patients through 3.1 lakh doctors) | ₹749 crore (41.9 lakh patients) | **₹749 crore** |
231	| SOM (the part we could win), year 3 | ₹3.7 crore (0.5% of SAM) | ₹2.1 crore (60 clinics x 200 patients) | **₹2.1 crore** |
232	| SOM, year 5 | ₹22.5 crore (3% of SAM) | ₹17.9 crore (400 clinics x 250 patients) | **₹17.9 crore** |
233	
234	The TAM used divides retail blood-pressure medicine sales by a private patient's yearly spend on one brand pill, giving 419.1 lakh patients. The SAM used takes 50% of them as reachable on a household smartphone and 20% as having a doctor who could enrol them (both ASSUMPTION), giving 41.9 lakh. Those two shares are the weakest inputs; the 50% is in line with smartphone access of 57.9% at ages 50-59 and 44.7% at 60-69 (2025 national survey, quoted second-hand) [D3-07-F11]. The model leaves out public-system patients, other conditions, device sales and every country outside India.
235	
236	#### The US$100 million-a-year test
237	
238	US$100 million a year is ₹942 crore at ₹94.25 to the dollar (rate on 13 Nov 2026). At ₹1,788 a patient a year that needs 52.7 lakh paying patients, more than the SAM holds. **On this model the test fails in India alone**: it needs 1.3 times the SAM (all OUR ARITHMETIC). Price moves the result as much as clinic count: at ₹99 a month the SAM used is ₹498 crore and 79.3 lakh patients are needed; at ₹299 it is ₹1,504 crore and 26.3 lakh; at Omada's revenue of about US$24.5 a member a month, 3,40,136 patients would do [D2-05-F23]. A public tier, shown apart, at ₹15 a month (ASSUMPTION) for the public programme's hypertension patients (chapter 1.3) would come to ₹756 crore a year (OUR ARITHMETIC), but a state would pay it only for results. OUR VIEW: blood pressure in India is the entry, not the whole company; the rest must come from more protocols on the same loop, a paid public tier, other countries or a higher price paid by an insurer, employer or medicine maker.
239	
240	#### Unit economics, per patient a month
241	
242	Every line is an ASSUMPTION from the build note. The clinic pays ₹149 (below Sugar.fit's ₹2,499 a month; OUR ARITHMETIC: ₹29,990 / 12). Costs are messages ₹15, cloud ₹5, reading cuff photos ₹2, and a health-worker call to silent patients ₹30, so the gross margin is ₹149 - 52 = ₹97, about 65% (OUR ARITHMETIC). Doctor time comes to about 4 minutes per 100 patients a month (6.5-8.5 proposals at 30 seconds each; OUR SIMULATION and ASSUMPTION), not costed. OUR VIEW: the health-worker call is the largest cost, and the margin holds only if doctors approve proposals without being paid per approval.
243	
244	#### Comparable companies and the funding climate
245	
246	Indian chronic-care firms in the notes lose money: Sugar.fit had revenue of ₹66.5 crore in FY25 and a loss of ₹42 crore [D2-05-F19]; Healthify had revenue of ₹228.76 crore in FY23 and a loss of ₹142 crore (aggregators) [D2-05-F22]. Abroad, Omada's revenue per member is US$294 a year (the monthly figure used above; OUR ARITHMETIC: 294 / 12), at a 76% gross margin [D2-05-F23], and no US medicine-adjusting programme publishes a price per member a month. US digital health raised US$7.4 billion in H1 2026 [D2-05-F16]; Indian health-tech raised US$310 million (headline only, tracker not named) [D2-05-F11].
247	
248	OUR VIEW: Omada's level of revenue a member is reached abroad only with employer and insurer payers. Indian comparables are small and loss-making.
249	
250	### 2.6 The rules
251	
252	> **In short.**
253	> - India's July 2026 guidance treats software that guides treatment as a medical device; a doctor-approved dose proposal could fall in Class A, B or C, which the regulator confirms.
254	> - In telemedicine, only a registered doctor may prescribe, and must deliver the prescription directly.
255	> - A study on patients needs permission and ethics approval first.
256	> - Abroad, each country pays through a clinician, and Germany ties part of the price to results.
257	
258	These are readings of the texts; open points remain questions for a lawyer and for CDSCO, India's medical-device regulator.
259	
260	#### Software as a medical device
261	
262	CDSCO issued its "Guidance Document on Medical Device Software" on 21 Jul 2026 [D2-04-F01]. India has four risk classes, A lowest and D highest, and the class follows the intended use stated in the label, website and promotion [D2-04-F02]. The grid for standalone software [D2-04-F03]:
263	
264	| Situation | Treatment or diagnosis | Drive clinical management | Inform clinical management |
265	|---|---|---|---|
266	| Critical | D | C | B |
267	| Serious | C | B | A |
268	| Non-serious | B | A | A |
269	
270	"Drive clinical management" covers information "to guide next diagnostics or next treatment interventions" [D2-04-F04]. A dose proposal that a doctor approves reads most naturally as "drive": Class B if hypertension is "serious", Class A if "non-serious", Class C if CDSCO reads it as "treatment" [D2-04-F06, D2-04-F49]. The guidance does not say where hypertension sits [D2-04-F05], and a patient-facing tool used without a professional can be moved up to "critical". CDSCO names a hypertension digital-therapeutics platform as medical device software [D2-04-F07], and India has no exemption for tools only a clinician sees [D2-04-F10]. OUR VIEW: clinician sign-off lowers the class; it does not take the software out of the device rules.
271	
272	#### Testing on patients
273	
274	A test licence (Form MD-13) covers making small quantities "for the purpose of Clinical Investigations or Test or Evaluation or Demonstration" [D2-04-F13]. A clinical investigation on patients needs CDSCO permission (MD-22/MD-23) [D2-04-F14], which the flowchart says is not mandatory for Class A [D2-04-F39]. Whether a pilot in which software drafts and a doctor decides counts as one is a question for counsel [D2-04-F50]. Trials must be registered on CTRI before the first patient, with ethics approval uploaded; whether a pilot in which the clinician decides needs this was NOT FOUND (search summary only) [D2-04-F45]. Fees and processing days were NOT FOUND [D2-04-F16].
275	
276	#### Who may prescribe and change a dose
277	
278	The Telemedicine Practice Guidelines (25 Mar 2020), clause 5.4, say platforms based on artificial intelligence or machine learning "are not allowed to counsel the patients or prescribe any medicines"; they may "assist and support" the doctor, but only a registered doctor may counsel or prescribe, and "the final prescription or counseling has to be directly delivered by the RMP" (registered medical practitioner) [D2-04-F17]. Whether later rules changed this in 2026 was not checked. In the national hypertension programme, community health officers delivered refills "based on the patient's prior prescription", and no law, rule or ministry order was found that lets a nurse, health officer or pharmacist change a dose under a standing order [D2-04-F18]. The Drugs and Magic Remedies Act 1954 bans advertisements suggesting a drug treats "High or low blood pressure", among other listed conditions; whether software counts as a "drug" under it is untested [D2-04-F31].
279	
280	OUR VIEW, for tonight's prototype: it is for test and demonstration, not a device on sale and not tested on patients; it uses open data, simulated patients or teammates' readings; a clinician approves every change and delivers the prescription, while the software only drafts; and it makes no claim that it treats or controls high blood pressure.
281	
282	#### Rules and payment abroad
283	
284	| Country | Device rule | How it is paid |
285	|---|---|---|
286	| United States | Insulin-titration software is a Class II device cleared by 510(k), for example My Dose Coach and d-Nav [D2-04-F24]; whether clinician-facing software that uses home cuff readings is a device at all is a question for counsel [D2-04-F22, D2-04-F23] | Medicare remote monitoring needs a face-to-face initiating visit from 1 Jan 2027 [D2-04-F26] |
287	| Germany | The DiGA route requires a positive care effect, with a decision in 3 months [D2-04-F28] | From 1 Jan 2026 at least 20% of the price must depend on measured outcomes [D2-04-F29, D1-05-F31] |
288	| Japan | CureApp HT, approved in April 2022 (search summary only), has been insured since 1 Sep 2022 as an add-on app that coaches lifestyle, not a dose change [D3-06-F19, D2-04-F37] | From 1 Jun 2026, 90 points a month in person or 78 online, plus 7,010 yen for the app (company release and a news report); the patient pays 30% (search summary only) [D2-04-F43, D3-06-F20]. Older figures differ: 7,010 yen (Jan 2024) or about 2,490 yen a month at a 30% patient share (2022), on different bases, unreconciled [D1-05-F33]; about 8,000 yen (search summary only) [D1-01-F57] |
289	
290	OUR VIEW: all three pay through a clinician, and Germany now ties part of the price to outcomes.
291	
292	Full detail: Appendix B (the clinical evidence and the programmes), Appendix C (the technology), Appendix D (every player) and Appendix E (money and rules).
293	
294	OUR VIEW: the research points one way. The treatment change, made by someone allowed to make it, is what works. India's programme has everything for it except a decision between visits. The technology to trust a home reading and bound a decision exists in open parts. No Indian service was found that does it, and no payer was found for it. The next chapter puts these findings together and weighs what to build.
295

## 2. What the research found

Chapter 1 showed a large, treatable population, a system that loses half of it between visits, and a market that stops before the dose. This chapter condenses what the research found, in plain words. It starts with the clinical evidence on what actually improves outcomes, then turns to how others have scaled care without specialists, what the technology can and cannot do, who is already doing this, where the money is and what the rules allow.

### 2.1 What actually improves outcomes

> **In short.**
> - Outcomes improved when a home reading led to a changed treatment, and mostly did not when the reading was only shown or turned into a reminder.
> - Who was allowed to change the dose mattered more than the electronics.
> - Raising adherence on its own did not move outcomes.
> - The same pattern holds in diabetes, heart failure, warfarin and asthma, and the known harms of dose stepping can be met with stop rules.

The trials sort into five rules. OUR VIEW: the sorting is ours; the numbers are from the notes.

**Rule 1. The reading must change the treatment.** Across 15 pooled trials (7,138 people, 12 months), self-monitoring of blood pressure alone lowered systolic pressure (the upper number, in mmHg, millimetres of mercury) by 1.0 mmHg against usual care: no effect. With intensive support (dose changes by doctors, pharmacists or patients, plus education or counselling), not dose changes alone, it fell 6.1 mmHg [D1-01-F05]. Where the dose itself moved, the falls were larger. In the UK trial TASMIN-SR (552 high-risk patients, randomised, meaning people got each treatment by chance), patients stepping their own dose by an agreed plan had systolic pressure 9.2 mmHg lower than under usual care at 12 months [D1-01-F02]. In the US trial HyperLink (450 patients, 16 clinics randomised as clusters, meaning whole clinics rather than single patients), pharmacists adjusting drugs from home readings got 57.2% controlled against 30.0% with usual care [D1-01-F04]. An independent US review by the Peterson Health Technology Institute (PHTI, October 2024) rated monitoring-only programmes "not clinically meaningful" and programmes where care teams adjust drugs "clinically meaningful and more rapid", against a threshold of a 5 mmHg fall in systolic pressure [D1-01-F39].

![Extra fall in systolic pressure against usual care, by what was done with the reading](adaptive-care-pictures/20-what-lowers-pressure.png)

*Chart: separate trials with different patients and end points, so compare the groups, not single bars [D1-01-F01, D1-01-F02, D1-01-F03, D1-01-F04, D1-01-F05, D1-01-F06, D1-01-F07].*

**Rule 2. Who is allowed to decide matters more than the electronics.** In the UK trial TASMINH4 (1,182 patients, 12 months), the family doctor adjusted doses in every arm, and sending home readings electronically instead of on paper added 1.2 mmHg, not significant (small enough to be chance) [D1-01-F03]. In rural China, the China Rural Hypertension Control Project (CRHCP: 326 villages, 33,995 people aged 40 and over) let village doctors start and step drugs by a standard protocol under physician supervision. At 18 months, 57.0% were under 130/80 against 19.9% with enhanced usual care [D1-01-F09]. After a median of 4 years, cardiovascular events were lower, with a hazard ratio (a risk ratio over time; below 1 means fewer events) of 0.75 at age 60 and over and 0.64 under 60. The programme also gave free or discounted drugs and paid village doctors incentives tied to control rates, so the effect cannot be credited to the protocol alone [D1-01-F38].

India has the null result that belongs here. mWellcare (40 community health centres, 3,698 people with hypertension, diabetes or both, 12 months, randomised by centre) gave nurses and doctors an app that prompted treatment steps during visits. Against enhanced usual care the systolic difference was 0.98 mmHg, not significant; both arms fell by about 13 mmHg [D1-01-F46]. OUR VIEW: it shows that a prompt at a visit adds nothing to a well-run protocol programme. It does not show that dose changes between visits fail: the app did not act on home readings or reach patients who never came back, and no Indian randomised trial of home readings driving a dose protocol was found (D1-01, NOT FOUND list).

![Share of patients under control with and without a programme that steps the dose](adaptive-care-pictures/21-share-controlled.png)

*Chart: three settings where someone other than a specialist was allowed to step the dose. The China programme also gave free or cheaper medicines and paid for results; the India figures are before and after among the 51% who returned, with no comparison group [D1-01-F04, D1-01-F09, D1-03-F10].*

**Rule 3. Adherence technology alone does not move outcomes.** Smart pillboxes or medication labels for tuberculosis (ASCENT, 23,483 patients, four countries) did not reduce poor outcomes against standard care [D1-02-F59]. Inhaler reminders for 220 New Zealand children raised adherence to 84% against 30% over 6 months, with no difference in school absence [D1-02-F01]. A blood-pressure reminder app (MedISAFE-BP, 411 US adults, 12 weeks) moved systolic pressure by 0.5 mmHg, not significant [D1-01-F06]. OUR VIEW: raising a dose that is not being taken is unsafe, so adherence is an input to the dose decision, not a product.

**Rule 4. Someone must pay for the outcome.** Chapter 1.5 told this side: apps and sensors sold on their own failed, while the firms that lasted are paid by employers and insurers, or sell a device that delivers the therapy.

**Rule 5. People stay when their own clinician is in it.** In eight remote US studies (over 1,00,000 participants), median retention was 5.5 days; referral by a clinician added 40 days, and payment 22 days (one study) [D1-02-F27]. OUR VIEW: a consumer app is the wrong shape.

#### What the loop changes, by kind

| What the loop changes | Home signal | Proof | Who decides |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Drug dose or protocol step | Cuff, fasting sugar, INR (a blood test of clotting time), weight | Strong | Patient on an agreed plan, pharmacist, nurse or health worker |
| 2. Food and behaviour | Glucose sensor, step count | Mixed | App, coach |
| 3. Exercise as the dose | Camera, pulse, effort rating | Matches in-person care | Therapist or app |
| 4. Therapy delivered by the device (closed-loop insulin pump) | Glucose sensor | Strong | Algorithm, within limits a clinician sets [D1-05-F41] |
| 5. Biofeedback (a body signal shown back to the patient) | Breathing or pulse sensor | Weak | Patient |

OUR VIEW: proof is strongest in kinds 1 and 4, where a drug dose with a known effect is changed and the signal is cheap, valid and fast. Kind 4 needs expensive hardware; kind 1 needs almost none.

#### The evidence by condition

| Condition | What works (headline) | Main caution |
|---|---|---|
| Blood pressure | Dose stepping from home readings by the patient, a pharmacist or a village doctor (rules 1 and 2); strongest proof, up to hard outcomes at 4 years | Leg swelling 32% against 22% with self-titration in TASMINH2 [D1-01-F01]; the China gain came with free drugs and incentives |
| Type 2 diabetes | A device computing the next insulin dose (d-Nav, 181 US adults, 6 months, against clinician support alone): HbA1c down 1.0 point against 0.3, with equal low-sugar events; several authors were maker-linked [D1-01-F13] | Low blood sugar. PHTI (March 2024) found US type 2 tools without a continuous glucose monitor "do not deliver clinically meaningful benefits" [D1-01-F40] |
| Heart failure | Fast dose stepping after discharge (STRONG-HF, 1,078 patients, 14 countries, against usual care): readmission or death at 180 days an adjusted 15.2% against 23.3% [D1-01-F27] | More side effects (41% against 29%), four visits in two months, lab tests. Telemonitoring without a mandated dose protocol was null in two US trials (1,653 and 1,437 patients) [D1-01-F32, D1-01-F33] |
| Warfarin (a blood thinner) | Testing INR at home and setting one's own dose: clots risk ratio (risk with treatment divided by risk without) 0.47 and deaths 0.55 against usual care; leaving the dose to the clinic gave no fewer deaths (0.94) [D1-02-F05] | The two approaches were not compared head to head |
| Asthma | Each reliever puff also raises the steroid dose (SMART): flare-ups risk ratio 0.68 (16 trials, 22,748 people), with no sensor [D1-02-F37] | A sensor inhaler system's benefit interval crossed 1 [D1-02-F02] |

Other areas repeat the pattern. Nurses stepping gout drugs to a target worked with no software at all [D1-02-F06]; tele-rehabilitation matches in-person care but does not beat usual care [D1-02-F03, D1-02-F07]; and guided breathing for blood pressure showed no effect once maker-linked trials were removed [D1-02-F11].

**Prescription apps and safety.** Software sold as a prescribed treatment has passed trials, yet most of the companies behind it failed (chapter 1.5), and none of the prescription apps in the research note changes a drug dose. The closest, Japan's CureApp HT, coaches lifestyle: in 390 untreated adults over 12 weeks it lowered 24-hour systolic pressure 2.4 mmHg more than lifestyle advice alone [D1-01-F07]. OUR VIEW: dose stepping by protocol has a good safety record when the protocol has stop rules. At 4 years in rural China, injurious falls, symptomatic low blood pressure, fainting and kidney outcomes did not differ between groups [D1-01-F38], and insulin-dose proposals in TeleDiab-2 (191 adults, 4 months) caused no severe low blood sugar [D1-01-F14]. The known costs, more minor side effects, leg swelling and low blood sugar, each need their own safety branch.

### 2.2 How care has been scaled without specialists

> **In short.**
> - India's programme already has a protocol, free drugs, a record and an overdue list; the dose step still waits for a doctor's visit.
> - Patients who keep attending do well on the protocol; the loss is among those who stop coming.
> - Abroad, the largest gains came where a non-doctor could step the dose, with free drugs or one pill.
> - Software was part of every working programme and the whole of none.

Chapter 2.1 showed that changing the dose works. This section asks how it has been delivered at scale without specialists.

#### India's hypertension programme in practice

IHCI runs a state protocol of 3 to 4 steps, amlodipine first (chapter 4.1 gives one state's steps); Punjab and Maharashtra order the steps differently at the second step [D3-05-F01, D1-06-F01, D1-06-F02]. Drugs are free, as 30-day refills at every facility level from health and wellness centres to district hospitals [D3-05-F02]. The open-source Simple app takes about 80 seconds to register a patient and 15 seconds for a follow-up, lists overdue patients with high-risk ones first, and offers one-click nurse calls and automated reminders [D3-05-F03]. Medical officers start amlodipine and review at 30 days; nurses register patients and record follow-up [D3-05-F06].

For patients who keep coming, the protocol works: in Punjab and Maharashtra, 70% and 76% of patients seen again were controlled on amlodipine 5 mg alone, and 75% and 81% after step 2 [D3-05-F04]. Across 159,292 patients who returned and stayed on protocol, control on clinic readings plateaued at 77% and 82%; about 43% of starters are missing from that count [D1-06-F04]. The drugs are cheap: amlodipine for the first two steps cut drug cost about 20%, from US$2.50 to US$2.05 per patient per year, not counting staff [D3-05-F05].

OUR VIEW: IHCI already has the protocol, free drugs, a record and an overdue list. It lacks a dose decision for the uncontrolled patient who does not go back to the doctor (chapter 1.3).

**Who changes the dose in practice.** Besides the refill rule in chapter 1.3, search summaries (only) say that state protocol text has the medical officer start and raise the dose, while the ANM (auxiliary nurse midwife) gives a month's medicines once pressure is controlled [D3-05-F31], and that a CHO (community health officer) screens, refers and follows up [D3-05-F30, D3-05-F13]. Whether a nurse or health officer may change a dose in law is open (chapter 2.6). OUR VIEW: design for a doctor approving every dose change.

**Tamil Nadu's doorstep scheme.** Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam, launched in August 2021, reported 1,86,13,872 beneficiaries by August 2024, with 92,59,821 people with hypertension given medicines (government figures, not audited; THEIR CLAIM) [D3-05-F14]. It refills; it does not step: no source says the dose is changed at the door [D3-05-F15]. OUR VIEW: high treatment with low control (chapter 1.2) is the gap a dose step addresses.

#### Programmes outside India

| Programme, size | Who steps the dose | Also in the package | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| China rural project (CRHCP) | Village doctors by protocol, physician-supervised | Free or discounted drugs; pay on control rate; audit; free home cuffs (search summary only) [D3-05-F21] | Chapter 2.1 |
| Lesotho; 103 villages, 547 people | Lay village health workers, by app | One fixed-dose pill | Under 140/90 at 12 months 58% against 48% (cluster trial against facility referral) [D3-05-F24] |
| IMPACT-BP, South Africa; 774 people | Nurses, remotely by app (not stated explicitly) | Health worker collects readings at home and delivers medicine | Systolic 7.9-9.1 mmHg lower at 6 months against standard care [D3-05-F27] |
| Nigeria; 60 centres, 21,922 people | Health workers under standing orders (search summary only) | Free drugs, then a US$1.60 co-pay a month; single pills; steady stock | Control 21.7% to 55.9% (2020-2023), no comparison group [D3-05-F22, D3-05-F23] |
| COBRA-BPS, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Sri Lanka; 2,645 people | Trained physicians; health workers monitored and referred | Home visits, counselling | Systolic 5.2 mmHg lower at 24 months (cluster trial) [D1-01-F37] |
| CARRS, India and Pakistan; 1,146 people with diabetes | Physicians, with software prompts | Care coordinators calling monthly | Combined target 18.2% against 8.7% at 28 months [D3-05-F18] (another note gives 8.1% for the comparison arm [D2-03-F14]); the chance of improving HbA1c, blood pressure and LDL cholesterol together doubled, risk ratio 2.1 at 12 months [D1-01-F23] |

OUR VIEW: the largest gains in control came where a non-doctor could step the dose, with free drugs or one pill; monitoring, counselling or prompts gained less or nothing. What these programmes changed, and software alone could not, was drug stock, authority for a non-doctor to change drugs (the PAHO HEARTS roadmap across 33 countries names nurse dose adjustment [D3-05-F28]), a person carrying medicine home, pay linked to control, and a person who phones and books visits. Software was part of every working programme and the whole of none.

### 2.3 What the technology can and cannot do

> **In short.**
> - A home reading can be several mmHg wrong for reasons unrelated to the cuff, such as posture; trusting it is the hard engineering.
> - Every working dose algorithm caps its actions and falls back to a standing plan when data is missing.
> - Language models make dose errors even when told to follow a protocol; they can read and speak, but should not decide.
> - Learning each patient's response is later work: no open data or simulator exists for blood-pressure drugs.

If changing the treatment is what works, the technology questions narrow to two: can a home reading be trusted, and can a decision be kept within safe bounds. OUR VIEW: the hard engineering is in trusting the home reading and in bounding the decision, not in the model that makes it.

#### Trusting a home reading

The American and European hypertension societies publish rules for home readings: how long to rest, how many readings, over how many days, and a lower threshold at home than in clinic; chapter 4.3 applies them [D2-02-F10, D2-02-F11, D2-01-F1]. Small mistakes move the number:

| Mistake | Effect, systolic / diastolic (mmHg) |
|---|---|
| Arm on the lap instead of on a desk | +3.9 / +4.0 (randomised crossover trial, 133 people, Baltimore) [D2-02-F16] |
| Arm hanging at the side | +6.5 / +4.4 (same trial) |
| Back not supported; legs crossed | +5 to +15 / +6; +5 to +8 / +3 to +5 (American Heart Association) [D2-02-F18] |
| Regular cuff on an arm that needs a large or an extra-large one | +4.8 or +19.5 systolic (randomised crossover trial, 195 people) [D2-02-F19] |

Noise has already hurt an Indian trial. SMARThealth India (a stepped-wedge cluster trial, in which groups of patients start the programme one after another; 18 clusters, rural Andhra Pradesh) found no blood-pressure effect, partly because "fluctuating BP values" made risk scores disagree, so only 37.2% of the cohort was exposed [D2-03-F17].

Getting the number in is also hard. No cuff sold in India was confirmed to use the standard Bluetooth blood-pressure service [D2-02-F3]. A purpose-trained reader of cuff-screen photos reached mean errors of 1.2/0.8 mmHg on 776 US images, but 82% of 7,205 images in a Guatemalan set were poor quality, and only Omron screens were tested [D2-02-F4]. No published test of a general vision-language model on these screens was found [D2-02-F8]. A Bluetooth home cuff, the Omron HEM-7156T, costs about ₹2,600 (2026 listings ₹2,593-3,500; search summary only) [D1-06-F31]. Cuffless blood pressure is not ready: the FDA cleared one cuffless monitor in July 2025 [D2-02-F23], but the European Society of Hypertension says there are "no generally accepted protocols" for validating such devices [D2-02-F25].

OUR VIEW: blood pressure is the one signal a household can measure with a validated, cheap device. Cuffless error is about the size of a dose step, so dose decisions stay on cuff readings, and every photo read must be shown back to the patient to confirm.

#### Algorithms that set a dose

Every dose algorithm in use is bounded. The do-it-yourself insulin system OpenAPS writes its safety rules down: it acts only through temporary basal rates, so if it stops, the pump returns to the normal plan; the rate is capped by the lowest of several limits, including "4x the current scheduled basal rate"; and missing or conflicting data sends it back to the pre-set plan [D2-03-F46]. The American Diabetes Association's 2025 insulin rule steps the dose every 3 days towards a fasting target and lowers it 10-20% after an unexplained low [D1-06-F16]; India's ICMR workflow gives targets but no titration schedule [D1-06-F17]. Blood-pressure ladders use fixed steps with a 30-day review, lab and pregnancy guards and referral at the end (chapter 4.1) [D1-06-F14].

People do differ. PHYSIC (randomised, double-blind, repeated crossover, 280 people, Sweden) found real between-person differences in drug response, worth about 4.4 mmHg if the drug were chosen per person [D2-03-F12], while a one-time "responder" label did not predict 12-month response in 608 Chinese patients [D2-03-F13]. OUR VIEW: every working dose algorithm caps its actions and falls back to a standing plan when data is missing; a ladder is the simplest case, and PHYSIC is the honest reason a later learning layer could add value.

#### A protocol as data, and decision support in India

A protocol written as data, not code, can be read by a clinician, tested branch by branch and swapped without changing the engine. No ready standard fits: WHO SMART Guidelines have no general hypertension kit [D2-03-F50]. Testing is the hard part: when the US VA re-encoded its hypertension decision support (ATHENA-HTN), 26 decision points gave 3,120 possible outputs, and 100 test cases covered "only 1% of the possible output combinations" [D2-03-F55].

Indian trials of decision support for clinicians are mixed. CARRS (chapter 2.2) was positive with care coordinators; mWellcare (chapter 2.1) [D2-03-F15] and SMARThealth (above) were null. IMPACT Diabetes (cluster randomised, 418 people, 9 months) gave ASHAs (village health workers) a tablet tool under physician supervision: HbA1c fell by 0.5 or more in 21.8% against 10.3% with usual care [D2-03-F18, D3-04-F17]. OUR VIEW: decision support alone did not beat a well-run programme in two Indian trials, so an engine must act between visits, not prompt during them, and ATHENA's 1% says to test on generated cases and replayed data, not only hand-written ones.

#### What language models may and may not do with doses

GPT-4, prompted with a hospital tacrolimus protocol on 300 simulated cases, made 13.9% "sentinel errors" in its first version; with stronger constraints and output checks the rate fell to 1.0%, and 13.3% of runs were not reproducible (OUR ARITHMETIC: 100 - 86.7) [D2-03-F38]. No completed randomised trial of a language-model coach with a blood-pressure or HbA1c outcome was found; two are registered [D2-03-F44]. Of the health models the large labs have built, only MedGemma, PaPaGei and HealthBench can be downloaded, and none sets doses [D2-03-F32, D2-03-F28, D2-03-F33].

OUR VIEW, following [D2-03-F38, D2-03-F40, D2-03-F46]: the model handles language only (reading the cuff photo, translation, speech); a fixed, tested engine makes every decision from the protocol file; code checks every output against the protocol; and a clinician approves every change.

#### Later work

Adaptive nudging, which learns when and what to send each person, has one head-to-head win, on steps, not on a clinical measure (DIAMANTE, 168 people, US) [D2-03-F10]. A "digital twin" (a model of one person that predicts their response) is further off for blood-pressure drugs. No open model of that response, no titration simulator, no open type 2 diabetes simulator and no large open dataset of home readings with medicine changes was found [D1-06-F42, D1-06-F43, D1-06-F30]. What can be tested on now is the programme's control-by-step figures [D1-06-F04] and open home blood-pressure series (the R `bp` package, GPL-3) [D2-03-F61]. OUR VIEW: each approved step in a loop gives one labelled example, readings before and 30 days after, which is the dataset a response model would need.

### 2.4 Who is already doing this

> **In short.**
> - In India, many programmes coach around a sensor; the one product found that changes a dose is a drug maker's insulin app of unknown status.
> - Abroad, lasting businesses are paid by employers, insurers or health systems, or sell a device that delivers the dose.
> - The nearest relatives of a home dose loop are a US company whose software is in a regulator's pilot, a UK company now wound up, and a Japanese cuff maker's UK tool.
> - Most money abroad goes to products that show data or coach; no funded home blood-pressure dose-step service was found.

Chapter 1.5 told why the market has not fixed the gap. This section maps who is in it, by adaptive depth.

#### India
