Searches for insulin titration found only My Dose Coach, and searches for inhaler plans, home heart-failure and kidney care, WhatsApp dose changes and GLP-1 dose companions found none that changes the dose. This was one agent's limited search, not proof of absence.

#### Abroad

Scaled companies abroad are paid by employers, insurers or health systems, or sell a device that delivers the therapy (chapter 1.5 gave Hinge Health and Insulet). Omada (US), paid by employers, plans and health systems, had revenue of $91.3M from 1,134,000 members in the quarter to 30 Sep 2026 and is listed and profitable [D1-05-F12, D1-05-F13]. Virta (US), where clinicians cut medicines, says its revenue is above $160M a year (THEIR CLAIM, Sep 2025) [D1-05-F18].

#### The nearest relatives

No funded startup of 2025 or 2026 was found whose funding page describes home blood-pressure dose steps by protocol. The nearest are these.

- **Cadence (US).** Remote vital signs for older adults; supervised AI agents support medicine changes under the partner medical group's protocols, and health systems pay; how far the AI decides alone is not stated. It raised a $100M Series C in June 2026 [D2-06-F1] and reports 100,000+ active patients and blood-pressure control up 70% relative (THEIR CLAIM) [D2-06-F2]. On 13 Aug 2026 it said its HypertensionOS, protocol-bound titration software for blood-pressure medicines, was selected for the FDA's TEMPO pilot, which "does not constitute FDA approval or clearance" (THEIR CLAIM) [D3-06-F31]. PHTI had named Cadence among the programmes where a team adjusts medicine [D1-05-F1].
- **Closed Loop Medicine (UK).** Its one blood-pressure trial (published 2024, company and university authors) adjusted amlodipine through an app in 205 adults over 14 weeks, with no comparison group; systolic fell 11 mmHg [D3-06-F09]. It also launched GLP-1 dose options for clinicians in the US (WeDosify, 18 Sep 2025) [D2-06-F24]. The company has been in members' voluntary liquidation (a solvent winding-up by shareholders) since 28 Apr 2026 [D3-06-F07].
- **Omron (Japan), in the UK.** The cuff maker's Hypertension Plus collates home readings and drafts a medication plan that the clinician accepts or modifies (search summary only; THEIR CLAIM) [D3-06-F35].

#### Prescribed apps and funded companies abroad

Germany is the one country with years of numbers on apps that doctors prescribe and public insurers pay for (called DiGA): about 1.9 million prescriptions in 2020-2025 [D1-05-F27], about EUR 400M paid by insurers in five years [D1-05-F28], and an average negotiated price of EUR 227 across 40 apps [D1-05-F29]; 18 of 81 listed apps were removed for lack of proven benefit (Sep 2026) [D1-05-F25]. Japan insures CureApp HT (chapter 2.6), but its prescription counts were NOT FOUND [D1-05-F36]. OUR VIEW: public payers will pay for prescribed apps, but increasingly for results.

Among 32 companies funded or launched abroad, the largest rounds went to Function ($298M), Hippocratic AI ($126M), Cadence and Nourish ($100M each), and only Cadence describes medicine changes [D2-06-F42, D2-06-F20, D2-06-F5]. Blood-pressure money buys sensors, not decisions: Biobeat, Aktiia and Vital Signals raised $50M, $42M and $15M+ for products that only show readings [D2-06-F36, D2-06-F37, D2-06-F38]. Only three of the 32 are clearly at depth 4 (Cadence, Twin Health and WeDosify). The frontier AI labs' consumer health features of 2026, such as ChatGPT Health (7 Jan) and Claude's health connectors (11 Jan), read phone health data and change no treatment [D2-06-F15, D2-06-F16]. None of the Y Combinator and a16z lines read mentions dose titration by rule [D2-06-F47, D2-06-F49, D2-06-F50].

OUR VIEW, the gap: abroad the pattern exists inside broad virtual clinics paid by US payers and for weight-loss medicines, and the low-income-country programmes found are protocol care, not device-linked dose loops [D1-05-F65]. Nobody funded sells a blood-pressure dose loop for a public programme run by health workers. These are one night's search results: a hospital, drug maker or state may run something unpublished.

### 2.5 The money

> **In short.**
> - Most money in blood-pressure care goes to medicines; a service priced near a pill would double the patient's bill, so usually someone else must pay.
> - No Indian payer was found for remote monitoring or digital therapy; our view is that a private clinic or hospital chain is the likeliest first payer.
> - On our own arithmetic the reachable Indian market is real but small for a venture fund, and the US$100 million-a-year test fails on India alone.
> - Indian chronic-care firms in the notes lose money; the profitable foreign ones are paid by employers and plans.

Chapter 1.5 showed who pays today. This section follows the rupee further.

#### What is spent today

India's retail medicine market was ₹2,45,943 crore in the year to March 2026 [D2-05-F02]. Blood-pressure medicines sold about ₹16,371 crore at retail chemists in the year to December 2025 (not hospital tenders or Jan Aushadhi; the page does not label the period explicitly) [D2-05-F01]. One amlodipine plus telmisartan 5/40 pill a day had a median price of ₹10.7 a tablet for a private brand, ₹1.5 for a Jan Aushadhi generic and ₹0.59 in the public programme (2019-20 prices). The private brand comes to about ₹3,906 a year, about ₹325 a month (OUR ARITHMETIC: ₹10.7 x 365); that is the cost of one brand pill, not a measured patient spend, and the paper's private range is about ₹2,500-5,100 a year [D2-05-F17]. No measured public-private split of treatment was found; a 2021 letter assumed 30% public [D2-05-F30]. OUR VIEW: a service near the price of one combination pill doubles the bill, so usually someone else must pay.

#### Who could pay in India

| Payer | What the notes have | Would they pay (OUR VIEW) |
|---|---|---|
| Patients | Chapter 1.5 | Some urban patients will; a monthly fee on top of medicines is hard for most |
| Clinics and hospital chains | The private sector gives about 70% of all outpatient care (authors' statement, 2021) [D3-07-F03] | Yes, if the loop keeps patients and refills inside their system |
| Medicine makers | Patient-support budgets NOT FOUND [D2-05-F40] | Possible, but a maker that sells the drug being stepped up has a conflict |
| Insurers | IRDAI's 2024 master circular says insurers should offer chronic and outpatient cover but does not mandate it [D2-04-F33] | Not yet: almost no outpatient cover |
| Employers | Could not be confirmed | Possible, with a slow sales cycle |
| States | Chapters 1.3 and 1.5; AB-PMJAY pays for hospital care only (search summary only) [D2-04-F47] | Largest pool, lowest price; only for proven results |

OUR VIEW: the first payer is a private clinic or hospital chain. Insurers become a payer only after outcome data exist.

#### Market size, counted two ways

All figures here are OUR ARITHMETIC from our market model, in rupees a year, at ₹149 a patient a month, ₹1,788 a year (ASSUMPTION, from the build plan). Each level is counted top-down and bottom-up, and the lower figure is used so the case does not rest on the kinder count.

![Market size, counted two ways](adaptive-care-pictures/23-market-size.png)

*Chart: the levels used after counting each two ways. OUR ARITHMETIC; several inputs are assumptions.*

| Level | Top-down | Bottom-up | Used (the lower) |
|---|---|---|---|
| TAM (total market): Indian adults on blood-pressure medicines | ₹7,494 crore (419.1 lakh private retail patients) | ₹9,969 crore (557.5 lakh treated adults, low case) | **₹7,494 crore** |
| SAM (the part we could serve): private patients a doctor could enrol on a household smartphone | ₹1,668 crore (93.3 lakh patients through 3.1 lakh doctors) | ₹749 crore (41.9 lakh patients) | **₹749 crore** |
| SOM (the part we could win), year 3 | ₹3.7 crore (0.5% of SAM) | ₹2.1 crore (60 clinics x 200 patients) | **₹2.1 crore** |
| SOM, year 5 | ₹22.5 crore (3% of SAM) | ₹17.9 crore (400 clinics x 250 patients) | **₹17.9 crore** |

The TAM used divides retail blood-pressure medicine sales by a private patient's yearly spend on one brand pill, giving 419.1 lakh patients. The SAM used takes 50% of them as reachable on a household smartphone and 20% as having a doctor who could enrol them (both ASSUMPTION), giving 41.9 lakh. Those two shares are the weakest inputs; the 50% is in line with smartphone access of 57.9% at ages 50-59 and 44.7% at 60-69 (2025 national survey, quoted second-hand) [D3-07-F11]. The model leaves out public-system patients, other conditions, device sales and every country outside India.

#### The US$100 million-a-year test

US$100 million a year is ₹942 crore at ₹94.25 to the dollar (rate on 13 Nov 2026). At ₹1,788 a patient a year that needs 52.7 lakh paying patients, more than the SAM holds. **On this model the test fails in India alone**: it needs 1.3 times the SAM (all OUR ARITHMETIC). Price moves the result as much as clinic count: at ₹99 a month the SAM used is ₹498 crore and 79.3 lakh patients are needed; at ₹299 it is ₹1,504 crore and 26.3 lakh; at Omada's revenue of about US$24.5 a member a month, 3,40,136 patients would do [D2-05-F23]. A public tier, shown apart, at ₹15 a month (ASSUMPTION) for the public programme's hypertension patients (chapter 1.3) would come to ₹756 crore a year (OUR ARITHMETIC), but a state would pay it only for results. OUR VIEW: blood pressure in India is the entry, not the whole company; the rest must come from more protocols on the same loop, a paid public tier, other countries or a higher price paid by an insurer, employer or medicine maker.

#### Unit economics, per patient a month

Every line is an ASSUMPTION from the build note. The clinic pays ₹149 (below Sugar.fit's ₹2,499 a month; OUR ARITHMETIC: ₹29,990 / 12). Costs are messages ₹15, cloud ₹5, reading cuff photos ₹2, and a health-worker call to silent patients ₹30, so the gross margin is ₹149 - 52 = ₹97, about 65% (OUR ARITHMETIC). Doctor time comes to about 4 minutes per 100 patients a month (6.5-8.5 proposals at 30 seconds each; OUR SIMULATION and ASSUMPTION), not costed. OUR VIEW: the health-worker call is the largest cost, and the margin holds only if doctors approve proposals without being paid per approval.

#### Comparable companies and the funding climate

Indian chronic-care firms in the notes lose money: Sugar.fit had revenue of ₹66.5 crore in FY25 and a loss of ₹42 crore [D2-05-F19]; Healthify had revenue of ₹228.76 crore in FY23 and a loss of ₹142 crore (aggregators) [D2-05-F22]. Abroad, Omada's revenue per member is US$294 a year (the monthly figure used above; OUR ARITHMETIC: 294 / 12), at a 76% gross margin [D2-05-F23], and no US medicine-adjusting programme publishes a price per member a month. US digital health raised US$7.4 billion in H1 2026 [D2-05-F16]; Indian health-tech raised US$310 million (headline only, tracker not named) [D2-05-F11].

OUR VIEW: Omada's level of revenue a member is reached abroad only with employer and insurer payers. Indian comparables are small and loss-making.

### 2.6 The rules

> **In short.**
> - India's July 2026 guidance treats software that guides treatment as a medical device; a doctor-approved dose proposal could fall in Class A, B or C, which the regulator confirms.
> - In telemedicine, only a registered doctor may prescribe, and must deliver the prescription directly.
> - A study on patients needs permission and ethics approval first.
> - Abroad, each country pays through a clinician, and Germany ties part of the price to results.

These are readings of the texts; open points remain questions for a lawyer and for CDSCO, India's medical-device regulator.

#### Software as a medical device

CDSCO issued its "Guidance Document on Medical Device Software" on 21 Jul 2026 [D2-04-F01]. India has four risk classes, A lowest and D highest, and the class follows the intended use stated in the label, website and promotion [D2-04-F02]. The grid for standalone software [D2-04-F03]:

| Situation | Treatment or diagnosis | Drive clinical management | Inform clinical management |
|---|---|---|---|
| Critical | D | C | B |
| Serious | C | B | A |
| Non-serious | B | A | A |

"Drive clinical management" covers information "to guide next diagnostics or next treatment interventions" [D2-04-F04]. A dose proposal that a doctor approves reads most naturally as "drive": Class B if hypertension is "serious", Class A if "non-serious", Class C if CDSCO reads it as "treatment" [D2-04-F06, D2-04-F49]. The guidance does not say where hypertension sits [D2-04-F05], and a patient-facing tool used without a professional can be moved up to "critical". CDSCO names a hypertension digital-therapeutics platform as medical device software [D2-04-F07], and India has no exemption for tools only a clinician sees [D2-04-F10]. OUR VIEW: clinician sign-off lowers the class; it does not take the software out of the device rules.

#### Testing on patients

A test licence (Form MD-13) covers making small quantities "for the purpose of Clinical Investigations or Test or Evaluation or Demonstration" [D2-04-F13]. A clinical investigation on patients needs CDSCO permission (MD-22/MD-23) [D2-04-F14], which the flowchart says is not mandatory for Class A [D2-04-F39]. Whether a pilot in which software drafts and a doctor decides counts as one is a question for counsel [D2-04-F50]. Trials must be registered on CTRI before the first patient, with ethics approval uploaded; whether a pilot in which the clinician decides needs this was NOT FOUND (search summary only) [D2-04-F45]. Fees and processing days were NOT FOUND [D2-04-F16].

#### Who may prescribe and change a dose

The Telemedicine Practice Guidelines (25 Mar 2020), clause 5.4, say platforms based on artificial intelligence or machine learning "are not allowed to counsel the patients or prescribe any medicines"; they may "assist and support" the doctor, but only a registered doctor may counsel or prescribe, and "the final prescription or counseling has to be directly delivered by the RMP" (registered medical practitioner) [D2-04-F17]. Whether later rules changed this in 2026 was not checked. In the national hypertension programme, community health officers delivered refills "based on the patient's prior prescription", and no law, rule or ministry order was found that lets a nurse, health officer or pharmacist change a dose under a standing order [D2-04-F18]. The Drugs and Magic Remedies Act 1954 bans advertisements suggesting a drug treats "High or low blood pressure", among other listed conditions; whether software counts as a "drug" under it is untested [D2-04-F31].

OUR VIEW, for tonight's prototype: it is for test and demonstration, not a device on sale and not tested on patients; it uses open data, simulated patients or teammates' readings; a clinician approves every change and delivers the prescription, while the software only drafts; and it makes no claim that it treats or controls high blood pressure.

#### Rules and payment abroad

| Country | Device rule | How it is paid |
|---|---|---|
| United States | Insulin-titration software is a Class II device cleared by 510(k), for example My Dose Coach and d-Nav [D2-04-F24]; whether clinician-facing software that uses home cuff readings is a device at all is a question for counsel [D2-04-F22, D2-04-F23] | Medicare remote monitoring needs a face-to-face initiating visit from 1 Jan 2027 [D2-04-F26] |
| Germany | The DiGA route requires a positive care effect, with a decision in 3 months [D2-04-F28] | From 1 Jan 2026 at least 20% of the price must depend on measured outcomes [D2-04-F29, D1-05-F31] |
| Japan | CureApp HT, approved in April 2022 (search summary only), has been insured since 1 Sep 2022 as an add-on app that coaches lifestyle, not a dose change [D3-06-F19, D2-04-F37] | From 1 Jun 2026, 90 points a month in person or 78 online, plus 7,010 yen for the app (company release and a news report); the patient pays 30% (search summary only) [D2-04-F43, D3-06-F20]. Older figures differ: 7,010 yen (Jan 2024) or about 2,490 yen a month at a 30% patient share (2022), on different bases, unreconciled [D1-05-F33]; about 8,000 yen (search summary only) [D1-01-F57] |

OUR VIEW: all three pay through a clinician, and Germany now ties part of the price to outcomes.

Full detail: Appendix B (the clinical evidence and the programmes), Appendix C (the technology), Appendix D (every player) and Appendix E (money and rules).

OUR VIEW: the research points one way. The treatment change, made by someone allowed to make it, is what works. India's programme has everything for it except a decision between visits. The technology to trust a home reading and bound a decision exists in open parts. No Indian service was found that does it, and no payer was found for it. The next chapter puts these findings together and weighs what to build.

     - Potassium rule (UKKA, F34): caution above 5.0 before starting; 5.5-5.9 recheck within 3 days; 6.0-6.4 recheck within 1 day and stop the RAS blocker; 6.5 or more admit.
     - The gap: US labels give no numbers, and the Telangana and Maharashtra IHCI sheets ask for no recheck after telmisartan (F04, F06, F57). The Gujarat HEARTS sheet itself was not opened in this note.

One North Indian centre saw hyponatraemia peak at 45% in the hot season (F62).
     - Starting any antihypertensive in older people: hip fractures 43% higher in the first 45 days (F48). In ALLHAT, amlodipine raised falls in the first year only (F49).
     - Intensive blood-pressure targets do not raise orthostatic hypotension in trials (F44).
     - Patients can reliably test themselves for a drop on standing at home (kappa 0.90, F50).
     - Practical point: put the safety checks (sodium, potassium, a sit-then-stand reading pair, a falls question) in the window right after each step.

  D4-02 is done. The evidence supports keeping 30 days as the default step, with a faster step justified only for the amlodipine 5 to 10 mg increase.
  
  **Note:** `C:\Users\Jaidityaa Jain\OneDrive\Desktop\TechSparks\research_notes\dtx\D4-02 How fast a dose change works.md`. I wrote only this file. Temporary downloads are in the scratchpad.
  
  **Facts:** 44 in total (D4-02-F01 to F44): 43 OPENED and 1 SNIPPET.
  - 15 of the OPENED facts rest on the abstract only. The fact line says "abstract only" in its source-date field; the OPENED field itself is plain OPENED.
  - F44 comes from a news report of the trial, not the paper.
  - The SNIPPET is F23, the ACC/AHA 2017 and 2025 wording on follow-up interval. The guideline pages returned HTTP 403, so that wording is not verified.
  
  **Searches used:** 11 of 35. Direct fetches did not count: openFDA/DailyMed labels, Europe PMC, the WHO PDF, the ISH PDF, the ESH journal page, the NICE page, state protocol PDFs and a Swedish telmisartan SmPC.
  
  **Three findings that matter most for the home BP step loop:**
  
  1. **Most of a dose change's effect arrives within 2 weeks, and nearly all by 4.**
     - A review of 18 trials found half of the full BP fall arrives in about 1 week (systolic 0.91 weeks, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.10), and drug class did not change the time course (F36).
     - If the curve is a simple exponential (assumed; the paper's equation was not opened), that means about 78% at 2 weeks and 95% at 4 (F37, our arithmetic).
     - The protocol's days 24 to 30 reading window therefore sees about 93 to 96% of the full effect.
     - A 14-day cycle read on days 8 to 14 would see only about 58 to 78%, so the loop would step up some patients whose current dose would have worked.
     - Steady state: amlodipine 7 to 8 days, chlorthalidone about 7 to 12, telmisartan about 4 to 5, HCTZ 1 to 3 (F01, F05, F08, F11).
  
  2. **Guidelines and labels allow faster steps for some drugs, but evidence that it helps is mostly observational.**
     - WHO 2021: monthly follow-up until target, a conditional recommendation on low-certainty evidence (F18).
     - ESH 2023: monthly, but notes 2-weekly visits gave earlier control in three observational studies and one small RCT, and says visit frequency should not follow "rigid rules" (F20).
     - India's Punjab IHCI sheet allows titration "at 15 days frequency if required" (F15); the Madhya Pradesh sheet says 30 days only (F16).
     - The amlodipine label says "wait 7 to 14 days between titration steps" (F03), and a 1987 trial titrated amlodipine every 2 weeks with only slight ankle oedema (F35).
     - The one RCT is small: 2-weekly protocol visits beat usual care at 12 months in 156 patients (F24).
     - Direct data on side effects of faster stepping are thin (F28, F31, F34).
     - In India's IHCI programme, 70 to 76% were controlled on amlodipine 5 mg and control plateaued at 77 to 82% from step 3 or 4 (F17).
  
  3. **Telmisartan and chlorthalidone are the drugs where a fast step is least safe to assume.**
     - Telmisartan: the US label puts maximal effect at about 4 weeks (F06). An EU-style SmPC says 4 to 8 weeks and warns about this before raising the dose (F43).
     - Chlorthalidone: in a small Indian ambulatory-BP trial (16 patients on 6.25 mg), the 24-hour fall was 6.74 mmHg at 4 weeks and 12.11 at 12 weeks, so about 56% of the 12-week effect was present at 4 weeks (F44).
     - Thiazide physiology fits this: the early fall comes from salt and water loss, the lasting fall from lower vessel resistance by 6 to 8 weeks (F39).
     - Office-BP data conflict and show most of the chlorthalidone effect by week 2 (F41, F10).
     - HCTZ 12.5 mg did not lower 24-hour BP in that Indian trial (F42). This matters because the protocol allows HCTZ when chlorthalidone is unavailable.
  
  **Gaps:**
  - No study gives weeks to maximal effect for amlodipine, or tracks BP after an amlodipine 5 to 10 mg step.
  - No trial compares 2-week with 4-week titration intervals on side effects.
  - The titration interval in the Nigeria triple-pill trial was not found.
  - South Asian time-course data are limited to IHCI and the small trial above.
  - The Gujarat sheet itself was not searched; the Punjab and Madhya Pradesh sheets were used instead.
</agent-message>

  I checked 45 fact IDs from D4-04 and wrote the note to `C:\Users\Jaidityaa Jain\OneDrive\Desktop\TechSparks\research_notes\dtx\D4-07 Claims check - biology part 2.md`. D4-04 itself was not edited. The table has 45 rows, each with exactly four cells, so the script can read it.
  
  **Counts:** 43 CONFIRMED, 2 CORRECTED, 0 CONTESTED, 0 NOT FOUND. Searches used: 0. Every source was a direct fetch:
  - PubMed `efetch` abstracts for the papers.
  - Europe PMC full text for the North India paper (PMC6924227) and the Kaiser cohort paper (PMC3196564).
  - openFDA label JSON and the DailyMed v2 service for the drug labels.
  - The NICE pages and the KDIGO, UKKA and IHCI PDFs, re-downloaded and read as text (same URLs as the note; no other route exists for these).
  
  **CORRECTED**
  1. **D4-04-F62 (North India hyponatraemia).** This one changes a product rule.
     - The "45%, 111 of 247" is not a rate among people taking diuretics. It is the share of 247 hospitalised low-sodium cases, from any cause, admitted in April to June. These were medical-ward inpatients in the case-control stage at the KGMU hospitals in Lucknow.
     - October to March held 46.6% (115 of 247) and July to September 9%. Per month, April to June is still busiest (about 37 cases a month against 19 and 7), so only a weak seasonal signal remains.
     - Diuretic use was not significant in the multivariate analysis, and the patients were middle-aged (mean about 50).
     - The note's "mainly loop diuretics likely" is wrong. Thiazides were the commonest class (45.9%, loop 35.8%) in the prevalence stage.
     - The prevalence (27%) and incidence (18% at 3 months, 29% at 6 months) figures are right.
     - So the "sodium test ... hot season" suggestion should rest on F58 and F61 (the first 30 days, older age, low weight, low potassium). Season can be a soft flag at most.
  2. **D4-04-F01 (telmisartan label source).** The quotes are verbatim, but the label is a PD-Rx Pharmaceuticals repackager listing (SPL v12, 4 Nov 2026). The product is made by Inventia Healthcare (Ambernath, India) and distributed by Ascend, revised March 2025. Alkem is not named.
  
  **Your eight items (all confirmed except item 4's 45% figure, above)**
  1. **Creatinine rule.**
     - The 30% thresholds and recheck timings are right, and so is the UK cohort (122,363 people; death IRR 1.35, 1.23 to 1.49, at a 20-29% rise).
     - "30% or more: investigate, then stop or reduce" is NICE NG203 1.6.21 wording. KDIGO says to continue unless creatinine rises "by more than 30% within 4 weeks", and gives no investigate-then-stop step.
     - NICE NG203 and KDIGO both apply only to adults with chronic kidney disease. UKKA 2.3 (grade 1A) is the only one of the three that covers every ACE inhibitor or ARB start, so the 1-to-2-week recheck rule should cite it.
  2. **UKKA potassium bands.** All bands and recheck windows match. Two wording details:
     - The 3-day recheck reads "or as soon as feasible", for mild hyperkalaemia "detected unexpectedly" in the community.
     - Stopping at 6 or more applies to patients "who do not meet the criteria for" the potassium binders patiromer or sodium zirconium cyclosilicate, not "unless on a binder".
     - Dates: original July 2020, updated October 2023 and July 2026. Its review date of October 2026 has passed.
  3. **IHCI sheets.** Confirmed: neither asks for a recheck after telmisartan. Both mention "close clinical and biochemical monitoring" for ACE inhibitor or ARB use in chronic kidney disease, but give no test or interval.
  4. **Thiazide hyponatraemia.** The Danish figures are confirmed exactly: HR 3.56 and 4.25 in the first 30 days, 1.26 and 1.29 after a year, and 3.51% to 3.83% at two years.
  5. **Falls.**
     - The hip-fracture IRR of 1.43 in the first 45 days and the ALLHAT year-1 amlodipine falls (HR 2.24 and 2.61) are confirmed.
     - The kappa of 0.90 is confirmed, but it comes from 25 people doing a lying-to-standing test. The product suggestion uses sit-then-stand, and NICE 1.1.7 says to repeat lying down if a seated test is negative.
  6. **Pregnancy.**

- **What changed on 14 November.** The 13 November document was written by many agents, one view per part (the doctor's, the engineer's, the business view and so on), and opened with its answer. The same facts were repeated across parts. This edition re-orders the same parts into one story (chapters 1 to 6) followed by an appendix (A to I) that holds the full detail, each topic in one place.
- **What did not change.** No new research was done. No fact, number, tag or judgement was added or changed. Repeated passages were removed and the wording was made plainer where that did not change the meaning.
- **How that was checked.** A script compared the new text with the 13 November parts: every fact ID cited in the old edition must be cited in the new one, no new ID may appear, and every number in the new text must also appear in the old text. The result is in the table of checks below.

### How this was made

- **When.** The night of 13 November 2026, between about 9:40 PM and midnight, India time, while the buildathon was running.
- **Who did what.** A coordinator (Claude Fable) planned the run, scored the options, wrote the argument, the Decision brief, parts A, L and M of the 13 November edition (their content is now in chapters 6 and 7 and the opening pages), and ruled where notes disagreed. Research agents gathered and recorded facts: Claude Opus for the clinical evidence, the build plans, the AI methods and the law; Claude Sonnet for the burden, the players, the market, the funded startups, the public voice, the scaled-care cases, the fund and the claims checks. Writers turned notes into parts: Fable for the challenge decoded, the strategist's view and what we could build; Opus for the rest. Separate agents drew the pictures and applied corrections.
- **Three rounds.** Round 1 answered "what to build tonight" (six notes). Round 2 produced the build plans, the methods, the rules, the market inputs and the funded-abroad tab (six notes, plus the coordinator's reading of the mentor's LinkedIn profile in the signed-in browser). Round 3 checked claims, filled gaps and added public voice, scaled-care cases, the fund's record and one late lead (eight notes).
- **A second session.** A side session opened by a "btw" message ran a duplicate research pass for about 13 minutes and then stopped. Its web notes were not used. Its two LinkedIn notes (L1 and L2) were, and are cited as "LinkedIn, read 13 Nov 2026".
- **The notes.** Everything is in `research_notes\dtx\`: the brief every agent followed (`D0-brief.md`), the notes (`D1-` to `D3-`), the scoring (`DT1-triage.md`), the argument (`DT2-spine.md`), the market model's output (`DT3-market-model.md`), the corrections and audit logs (`C1-` to `C3-` files) and the LinkedIn notes.
| Web searches | Research agents, three rounds | About 345 searches; most trial and protocol checks used direct fetches instead |
| Links | Every distinct source link in the 13 November edition requested once by script, 13 Nov 2026 about 11 PM | 494 links: 439 answered; 46 refused an automated request (LinkedIn and some news and journal sites; they open in a browser); 6 did not connect; 3 returned "not found" to the script (two US regulator pages, which often refuse scripts, and one news page) |

Most facts in the register below were read by one agent only and are marked "not re-checked". The checks were aimed at the facts that carry the argument, the market model and the protocol files.

### What was not found

Each appendix ends with its own list. The gaps that matter most for decisions:

- An Indian trial of home readings driving dose steps.
- A measured split of public and private treatment for high blood pressure.
- Current counts of specialists, and of private general doctors and clinics.
- Any Indian payer for remote monitoring or a digital therapeutic.
- A legal basis for a nurse or community health officer changing a dose.
- Prices paid to medicine-adjusting programmes in the United States.
- Uptake of the insured blood-pressure app in Japan.
- The buildathon's judging criteria.

content.content:
### 2.7 The biology underneath (new research, 14 Nov)

> **In short.**
> - Each protocol drug pulls a different lever, so adding a drug does far more than raising a dose, and step 4 adds almost nothing.
> - Every drug is at a steady level well before the day 24-30 readings, so the 30-day step fits the biology.
> - A step moves pressure less than the natural noise between two monthly means, so the loop must judge where the mean sits, with enough days, not how far it moved.
> - Each safety check has a mechanism and a time window; the body gives no cheap sign that amlodipine or telmisartan was taken.

Sections 2.1 to 2.6 rest on trial results and policy texts. This section, researched on 14 November after the rest of the document, adds the physiology underneath: why a step works, how fast, how much readings move on their own, why each safety check exists, and how to tell whether a medicine was taken. It is new research, and its main facts were re-checked by a second agent.

**Three levers.** Amlodipine relaxes the muscle of the smallest arteries [D4-01-F17]. Telmisartan blocks angiotensin II, the hormone that tightens them and drives aldosterone [D4-01-F20]. Chlorthalidone makes the kidney pass more salt and water [D4-01-F23]. The families add up, and partly cancel each other's counter-reactions: a thiazide raises renin and aldosterone, a counter-response that the ARB (angiotensin receptor blocker) blocks [D4-01-F22]. So doubling a dose gives only about one fifth of the extra fall that adding a second family gives [D4-01-F09]. Priced along the Gujarat ladder from the US combination label (1,461 patients, 8 weeks), step 2 adds about 5.3 mmHg systolic, step 3 about 4.0 and step 4 only 1.7 (OUR ARITHMETIC) [D4-01-F49]; in 947 patients not controlled on amlodipine 10 mg, telmisartan 80 mg did 0.2 mmHg better than 40 mg [D4-01-F50]. Step 2 has a cost: ankle swelling rises from 3.0% at 5 mg to 10.8% at 10 mg [D4-01-F19], and adding telmisartan to amlodipine 5 mg instead lowered pressure more, with swelling in 4.3% against 27.2% [D4-01-F51].

**Who responds to what.** People do differ, but mainly between two groups: a renin-angiotensin blocker on one side, amlodipine or a thiazide on the other (chapter 2.3 gave PHYSIC's size) [D4-01-F02, D4-01-F04]. Salt shifts the odds: a salty diet blunts renin-angiotensin blockers more than calcium blockers [D4-01-F13], and in north-east India 47.6% of people with high pressure were salt-sensitive [D4-01-F47]. For South Asians, 16 small trials, mostly Indian, found no difference between families [D4-01-F11]. Gene tests are not usable: the best single variant moves response by about 3 mmHg, and polygenic scores predict nothing [D4-01-F35, D4-01-F34]. And one patient's change after one step is mostly noise: in 28,281 trial patients only 3% of the apparent spread in response was real [D4-03-F55].

**How fast a step works.** Amlodipine reaches a steady blood level in 7-8 days [D4-02-F01], telmisartan in about 4-5 and chlorthalidone in about 7-12 (OUR ARITHMETIC from their half-lives) [D4-02-F05, D4-02-F08]. Across 18 trials, half of a first drug's full effect arrived in about a week [D4-02-F36]. On an assumed curve shape, readings on days 24-30 see about 80-96% of the full effect, and a 14-day step would see only 48-78% (OUR ARITHMETIC; the paper's equation could not be checked) [D4-02-F37]. Telmisartan's labels disagree on the maximum, about 4 weeks in the US and 4-8 weeks in a European text [D4-02-F06, D4-02-F43], and in a small Indian trial chlorthalidone's 24-hour effect was still growing at 12 weeks [D4-02-F44]. Punjab's sheet already allows 15-day steps "if required" [D4-02-F15]; Madhya Pradesh's does not [D4-02-F16]. Faster stepping has mostly observational support [D4-02-F25], and in the one trial with side-effect numbers (Nigeria, 300 adults) the faster arm had more early kidney-function falls and low potassium (corrected in the claims check) [D4-02-F34]. OUR VIEW: 30 days is right for the Gujarat steps; a shorter step is defensible only for amlodipine 5 to 10 mg.

**How much readings move on their own.** A single home reading in treated patients varies with an SD (standard deviation) of 11.8 mmHg within a week [D4-03-F10]. Averaging helps: between two weekly means in untreated adults, a real change must be about 12.5 mmHg for 3-day means and 8.5 mmHg for 7-day means (OUR ARITHMETIC) [D4-03-F34], and treated older patients vary more (claims check). A step's 2-6 mmHg is smaller than this, so the loop should judge where the mean sits against 135/85, with 7 days when it is near the line [D4-03-F02], not how far it moved. UK self-titration trials changed a drug only after two consecutive months above target [D4-03-F13, D4-03-F56]. Indian winter readings ran 9-11 mmHg above summer, though these were readings by nurses or investigators, not home cuffs [D4-03-F31, D4-03-F32], and patients picked for a high reading drift down on their own (regression to the mean) [D4-03-F26]. Chapter 1.4's GRAND percentages are of the 1,578 patients analysed, not of all 1,920 enrolled (corrected in the claims check) [D3-04-F09, D4-03-F40].

**Why each safety check exists.** Telmisartan relaxes the vessel leaving each kidney filter, so filtration pressure falls and creatinine rises a little, mostly in the first 2 weeks [D4-04-F26, D4-04-F27]. The UK Kidney Association rechecks creatinine and potassium 1-2 weeks after every ARB start or dose rise [D4-04-F34]; the Indian state sheets opened ask for no recheck [D4-04-F57]. Even rises under 30% went with higher death rates in UK records, though they may mark sicker patients [D4-04-F22]. High potassium can stop the heart, and the ECG can look normal [D4-04-F35]. In pregnancy an ARB stops the fetus making urine in the second and third trimesters, so the amniotic fluid drains and the lungs cannot grow [D4-04-F02, D4-04-F56]; NICE says stop within 2 working days and switch [D4-04-F29]. Thiazides cause low sodium most often in the first 30 days and in older, lighter people [D4-04-F58, D4-04-F61]. Among people over 60, 22.2% have a pressure drop on standing [D4-04-F39], and hip fractures rise in the 45 days after starting any blood-pressure drug [D4-04-F48]. A reading of 180/110 without symptoms is urgency, not emergency, which means organ damage [D4-04-F70]: patients sent home had no major heart events in 7 days [D4-04-F68], and long-standing high pressure resets the brain's protection of its blood flow to higher pressures [D4-04-F72] (OUR VIEW: an argument against lowering it fast at home).

**Lab tests and signs of intake.** The tests that move within a 30-day cycle are creatinine and potassium, plus sodium at the thiazide step; HbA1c moves over 2-3 months, and NT-proBNP is a district-hospital test for suspected heart failure [D4-05-F37, D4-05-F35]. A primary health centre runs creatinine, urea and uric acid, but sends potassium and urine albumin to a hub [D4-05-F39]. On adherence, drug assays abroad found about 1 in 3 patients with resistant hypertension not taking their drugs (31.2% pooled) [D4-05-F01], and a Brazilian clinic found 90.1% adherent by questionnaire against 32.4% by urine test [D4-05-F07]. No Indian assay study was found [D4-05-F15]. Amlodipine and telmisartan leave no mark on the pulse [D4-05-F16, D4-05-F18]; only the thiazide leaves a weak chemical trace, lower potassium and higher uric acid [D4-05-F22]. Cheap reminder devices did nothing for 53,480 US patients [D4-05-F24], while blister packs raised pills taken by 11% [D4-05-F46].

OUR VIEW: the biology fits the loop's shape and points to five additions: expected effects per step, profile fields, adherence checks beyond self-report, a reading rule sized to the noise, and a safety window after each step. Chapter 4.9 lists them as product features, and Appendix I holds the full detail.

Full detail: Appendix B (the clinical evidence and the programmes), Appendix C (the technology), Appendix D (every player), Appendix E (money and rules) and Appendix I (the biology, new research).

**How fast a step works.** Amlodipine reaches a steady blood level in 7-8 days [D4-02-F01], telmisartan in about 4-5 and chlorthalidone in about 7-12 (OUR ARITHMETIC from their half-lives) [D4-02-F05, D4-02-F08]. Across 18 trials, half of a first drug's full effect arrived in about a week [D4-02-F36]. On an assumed curve shape, readings on days 24-30 see about 80-96% of the full effect, and a 14-day step would see only 48-78% (OUR ARITHMETIC; the paper's equation could not be checked) [D4-02-F37]. Telmisartan's labels disagree on the maximum, about 4 weeks in the US and 4-8 weeks in a European text [D4-02-F06, D4-02-F43], and in a small Indian trial chlorthalidone's 24-hour effect was still growing at 12 weeks [D4-02-F44]. Punjab's sheet already allows 15-day steps "if required" [D4-02-F15]; Madhya Pradesh's does not [D4-02-F16]. Faster stepping has mostly observational support [D4-02-F25], and in the one trial with side-effect numbers (Nigeria, 300 adults) the faster arm had more early kidney-function falls and low potassium (corrected in the claims check) [D4-02-F34]. OUR VIEW: 30 days is right for the Gujarat steps; a shorter step is defensible only for amlodipine 5 to 10 mg.

**How much readings move on their own.** A single home reading in treated patients varies with an SD (standard deviation) of 11.8 mmHg within a week [D4-03-F10]. Averaging helps: between two weekly means in untreated adults, a real change must be about 12.5 mmHg for 3-day means and 8.5 mmHg for 7-day means (OUR ARITHMETIC) [D4-03-F34], and treated older patients vary more (claims check). A step's 2-6 mmHg is smaller than this, so the loop should judge where the mean sits against 135/85, with 7 days when it is near the line [D4-03-F02], not how far it moved. UK self-titration trials changed a drug only after two consecutive months above target [D4-03-F13, D4-03-F56]. Indian winter readings ran 9-11 mmHg above summer, though these were readings by nurses or investigators, not home cuffs [D4-03-F31, D4-03-F32], and patients picked for a high reading drift down on their own (regression to the mean) [D4-03-F26]. Chapter 1.4's GRAND percentages are of the 1,578 patients analysed, not of all 1,920 enrolled (corrected in the claims check) [D3-04-F09, D4-03-F40].

**Why each safety check exists.** Telmisartan relaxes the vessel leaving each kidney filter, so filtration pressure falls and creatinine rises a little, mostly in the first 2 weeks [D4-04-F26, D4-04-F27]. The UK Kidney Association rechecks creatinine and potassium 1-2 weeks after every ARB start or dose rise [D4-04-F34]; the Indian state sheets opened ask for no recheck [D4-04-F57]. Even rises under 30% went with higher death rates in UK records, though they may mark sicker patients [D4-04-F22]. High potassium can stop the heart, and the ECG can look normal [D4-04-F35]. In pregnancy an ARB stops the fetus making urine in the second and third trimesters, so the amniotic fluid drains and the lungs cannot grow [D4-04-F02, D4-04-F56]; NICE says stop within 2 working days and switch [D4-04-F29]. Thiazides cause low sodium most often in the first 30 days and in older, lighter people [D4-04-F58, D4-04-F61]. Among people over 60, 22.2% have a pressure drop on standing [D4-04-F39], and hip fractures rise in the 45 days after starting any blood-pressure drug [D4-04-F48]. A reading of 180/110 without symptoms is urgency, not emergency, which means organ damage [D4-04-F70]: patients sent home had no major heart events in 7 days [D4-04-F68], and long-standing high pressure resets the brain's protection of its blood flow to higher pressures [D4-04-F72] (OUR VIEW: an argument against lowering it fast at home).

**Lab tests and signs of intake.** The tests that move within a 30-day cycle are creatinine and potassium, plus sodium at the thiazide step; HbA1c moves over 2-3 months, and NT-proBNP is a district-hospital test for suspected heart failure [D4-05-F37, D4-05-F35]. A primary health centre runs creatinine, urea and uric acid, but sends potassium and urine albumin to a hub [D4-05-F39]. On adherence, drug assays abroad found about 1 in 3 patients with resistant hypertension not taking their drugs (31.2% pooled) [D4-05-F01], and a Brazilian clinic found 90.1% adherent by questionnaire against 32.4% by urine test [D4-05-F07]. No Indian assay study was found [D4-05-F15]. Amlodipine and telmisartan leave no mark on the pulse [D4-05-F16, D4-05-F18]; only the thiazide leaves a weak chemical trace, lower potassium and higher uric acid [D4-05-F22]. Cheap reminder devices did nothing for 53,480 US patients [D4-05-F24], while blister packs raised pills taken by 11% [D4-05-F46].

OUR VIEW: the biology fits the loop's shape and points to five additions: expected effects per step, profile fields, adherence checks beyond self-report, a reading rule sized to the noise, and a safety window after each step. Chapter 4.9 lists them as product features, and Appendix I holds the full detail.

Full detail: Appendix B (the clinical evidence and the programmes), Appendix C (the technology), Appendix D (every player), Appendix E (money and rules) and Appendix I (the biology, new research).

content.text:
I've rebuilt the document as one story with an appendix behind it, and added the biology research in its own clearly marked places. The new file is `SPARK Night 2026 - adaptive care challenge, story edition.pdf` (and `.md`), next to the original, which is untouched.

**How it reads now (215 pages)**

| Pages | Part |
|---|---|
| 1–3 | What this is, how the document is laid out, what to read for your role. The answer is not given up front. |
| 4–12 | **1. The problem**, told as a story: what the fund asks, who it affects, why care breaks down between visits, what patients and doctors say publicly, and why the market hasn't fixed it. |
| 13–27 | **2. What the research found.** Each section opens with an "In short" box, then plain-language detail. Section 2.7 is the new biology. |
| 28–33 | **3. Analysis**: the thesis, where to play and how to win, the seven options and their scores. The choice of what to build comes out at the end of this chapter. |
| 34–41 | **4. The product**, with the mock-up screens. Section 4.9 lists the product features the biology suggests. |
| 42–46 | **5. The MVP** |
| 47–50 | **6. Recommendation, risks and open questions** (your old L) |
| 51–53 | **7. Method and limits** (your old M) |
| 54–159 | **Appendices A–I**: the heavy detail, one topic per appendix, following the story's order. **I is the biology deep dive** (p. 144). |
| 160–215 | **Appendix J**: the claim register |

**Did any information change?** A script compared the new version with the old parts:
- All 587 original facts are still cited.
- No number was added, apart from the biology research and one correction.
- Each repeated fact is now explained once.

**The one correction.** The biology claims check found an error in the old document. In the GRAND study, the percentages are shares of the 1,578 patients analysed, not the 1,920 enrolled. I fixed it in all three places it appears and marked each fix as corrected on 14 November.

**The biology research.** It covers 284 new facts, mostly from primary papers, drug labels and guidelines. A second agent re-opened 183 of them: 175 confirmed, 5 corrected. The findings your biology teammate will care about most:
- **Step 4 barely helps.** Raising telmisartan from 40 to 80 mg lowers pressure only about 0.2 mmHg more. Adding a drug does about five times more than doubling a dose.
- **The 30-day step fits.** Half of a dose change's effect shows up in about a week. A 14-day step would act before the full effect is visible; there is a case for it only on the amlodipine 5 to 10 mg step.
- **One step is smaller than the natural noise.** A step moves pressure 2–6 mmHg, less than home averages drift from month to month on their own. So the loop should judge where the average sits against 135/85, using 7 days of readings near the line, rather than how far it moved.
- **A safety gap in the Indian sheets.** The Telangana and Maharashtra protocol sheets ask for no kidney or potassium blood test after telmisartan starts. The UK Kidney Association rechecks both 1–2 weeks after every start or dose increase.
- **The body won't show whether the medicine was taken.** Amlodipine and telmisartan leave no sign in the pulse. In drug tests abroad, about 1 in 3 patients whose pressure stays high despite treatment were not taking their pills. No Indian study of this was found.

These are written as suggestions in Appendix I. I did not change the protocol file or the MVP design, because that is for the team and a clinician to decide.

Two small things I left alone: three verbatim quotes still contain words the style rules ban (an exclamation mark in the mentor's LinkedIn comment, "cutting-edge" and "underutilised"). Changing them would alter the quotes.
